📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architectural styles are often identified through a familiar set of characteristics: particular forms, materials, proportions, and decorative elements. Yet these characteristics do not always remain tied to the traditions from which they originate. A classical column may appear on a self-built house, a modernist ceramic composition may be reproduced across a residential façade, or a chalet may become part of a multistory commercial building. Each retains something recognizable from its precedent, although its application reflects a different set of architectural decisions.

Architectural styles are often identified through a familiar set of characteristics: particular forms, materials, proportions, and decorative elements. Yet these characteristics do not always remain tied to the traditions from which they originate. A classical column may appear on a self-built house, a modernist ceramic composition may be reproduced across a residential façade, or a chalet may become part of a multistory commercial building. Each retains something recognizable from its precedent, although its application reflects a different set of architectural decisions.

It has been revealed that these transformations also raise questions about how architectural identity develops. The meanings associated with a particular style or building element are influenced by the people who adopt it, the construction methods available to them, and the cultural associations they bring to its use. Through individual choices and repeated adaptations, references that once belonged to specific architectural traditions can become part of expressions associated with entirely different places and communities.

According to recent reports, across Latin America, this process is visible in buildings whose architectural character has developed through the reinterpretation of existing references. In Mexico, self-built houses combine elements from different residential traditions; in Brazil, homeowners and builders have developed a regional expression through adaptations of modernist ceramic façades; and in Bolivia, Andean cultural references and European residential forms are incorporated into contemporary mixed-use buildings. What emerges from these adaptations is an architectural vocabulary shaped by the cultural references, construction practices, and aspirations of the people who develop it.

Architectural References in Mexico's Self-Built Homes.

Sources indicate that across parts of Mexico, self-built houses incorporate architectural elements associated with different styles and residential traditions. Classical columns, turrets, arches, domes, and elaborate rooflines appear in combinations that bring together features of European historical architecture and American suburban housing. Their proportions, ornamentation, and materials vary according to the preferences of individual homeowners and the construction methods available to local builders. These combinations are visible in Arquitectura Libre, photographer Adam Wiseman's documentation of self-built houses, many financed through remittances from the United States.

Modernism Reinterpreted in Pará.

Industry observers note that during the 1950s and 1960s, homeowners in Belém, Brazil, began incorporating the geometric compositions and ceramic panels associated with Brazilian modernism into their own residential façades. Modernist artists such as Athos Bulcão and Cândido Portinari had established prominent examples of decorative ceramic work, while local builders developed variations of these references using mosaics assembled from broken tiles. The resulting expression became known as Raio-que-o-parta.

During the 1950s and 1960s, homeowners in Belém, Brazil, began incorporating the geometric compositions and ceramic panels associated with Brazilian modernism into their own residential façades. Modernist artists such as Athos Bulcão and Cândido Portinari had established prominent examples of decorative ceramic work, while local builders developed variations of these references using mosaics assembled from broken tiles. The resulting expression became known as Raio-que-o-parta.

The expression initially appeared on houses belonging to wealthier families, before spreading to other residential neighborhoods. Homeowners often concentrated the decorative treatment on the platibanda, the parapet concealing the pitched roof from the street. Modifying this element allowed families to introduce modernist references without substantially altering the structure or organization of their houses. The façade became a visible expression of modernity, adapted to the scale and resources of individual residences.

Industry observers note that the use of broken ceramic tiles also influenced the composition of the mosaics. Fragments were arranged into lightning bolts, arrows, curves, and figurative patterns, with colors and geometric arrangements varying between houses. According to accounts documented by the Rede Raio que o Parta, tiles damaged during transportation along the Belém-Brasília highway were reportedly resold at reduced prices, making the material accessible to more families. Local mestres de obras, or master builders, worked with homeowners to determine the decorative treatment, introducing individual variations into a recognizable set of geometric and material references.

Through the repetition and modification of these elements, Raio-que-o-parta developed a regional architectural language associated specifically with Pará. Its modernist origins remained visible, while the compositions developed through local construction practices acquired their own characteristics. In 1966, art historian Donato Mello Júnior criticized these façades during a speech to the first graduating architecture class at the Federal University of Pará, using the term Raio-que-o-parta, roughly equivalent to "to hell with it." Architects Cybelle Salvador Miranda and Ronaldo Nonato Marques de Carvalho later adopted the name in their research beginning in 2009, documenting the architectural significance of the compositions developed by homeowners and builders.

Andean References in Contemporary Architecture.

In a recent development, in El Alto, Bolivia, the buildings known as cholets combine references from Andean cultural traditions with residential forms associated with European architecture. Developed prominently by Freddy Mamani since the early 2000s, these multistory buildings incorporate commercial premises, rental apartments, event halls, and private residences. Their architectural expression draws on Tiwanaku iconography and Aymara textile traditions, incorporating geometric patterns and saturated colors into contemporary construction.

The pitched-roof chalet introduces another architectural reference into these compositions. Shops typically occupy the ground floor, with event halls and rental apartments distributed across the intermediate levels. The owner's private residence sits on the rooftop, often in the form of a chalet. Traditionally associated with detached residential architecture, this form acquires a different position and use within El Alto's mixed-use buildings. The arrangement allows owners to combine their commercial activities and domestic lives on the same property, while giving the residence a prominent position above the other programs.

Sources indicate that facades once dismissed for their ornament are now studied as part of Latin America's architectural history. In Belém, the tile-shard houses that professionals once ridiculed became the subject of preservation efforts, and in November 2025 a municipal law declared Raio-que-o-parta intangible cultural heritage. Of roughly 300 documented houses, about 100 still keep their mosaics.

Outside Belém, recognition has come mostly from abroad. Copias del abandono was shown in the Mexican Pavilion at the 2021 Venice Biennale, and in 2018, Mamani built a replica of one of his event halls at the Fondation Cartier in Paris. Both moved buildings made for everyday life in Tlaxcala and El Alto into galleries, where visitors see the architecture without the uses that shaped it.

The changes that preservation tries to limit are the same kind of decisions that produced Raio-que-o-parta in the first place. Protecting these houses means deciding whether their history includes the alterations still being made to them.

Side stitch, stomach cramp, side ache — whatever you wanna call it, that mid-run pain in your tum can seriously *cramp* your runner’s high.

Recent findings suggest that this pesky prob that plagues runners and athletes all over has a scientific name: Exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP). Though experts don’t know exactly what causes it, they have some ideas and tips about how to stop it.

Before you double-over during your next marathon, here’s what to know.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod notes tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

Recent findings suggest that this common prob has been around for ages — the first historical mention is from ancient Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder. Yet, scientists still haven’t reached a consensus on its exact cause. We know that it affects up to 70% of runners each year.

It’s also more likely to occur on the right side.

A stiff spine or poor posture (according to older research from 2010) could contribute to side stitches – but TBH, the pros don’t know for sure.

It has been revealed that according to a 2022 review, researchers also think a side stitch might be caused by your right foot hitting the ground while you breathe out, irritating a phrenic nerve. Researchers think this, in turn, may bother the lining of your abdomen (particularly on the lower right side). Since most people are right-foot dominant, this is one possible explanation.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a massive race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” mentioned Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” remarked Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”.

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

According to recent reports, text description provided by the architects. In Veneux-les-Sablons, south-east of Paris, the church of Saint-Philippe-et-Saint-Jacques reopens ten years after the fire that partly destroyed it in 2016. Built in 1828 by subscription among the villagers, it had been enlarged in 1959 by a second nave set at right angles to the first. The fire destroyed that extension and most of the roof of the original nave. The Town of Moret-Loing-et-Orvanne decided to restore the church and rebuild its extension as a shared building: the historic nave remains a place of worship, the new extension becomes a cultural hall.

According to recent reports, certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

According to recent reports, but this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

Industry observers note that besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that problem with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi indicates.

Sources indicate that nielsen also takes matter with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a massive, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she claims.

Industry observers note that in other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi notes. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

“Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi states—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.).

That said, this matter can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen states.

In a recent development, in Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she says. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related problems like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same issue, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

In a recent development, given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.).

“In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen claims. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

On the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen indicates—and “protein is a big bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she says. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

In a recent development, even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one massive downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen notes. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

“Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen states. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.).

It has been revealed that “Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi says. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.

Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a fresh pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.
  • With the exhibition, the UK-based collective stated it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.
  • The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the newly introduced pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a fresh pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective stated it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the newly introduced pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.

The blue hue was manufactured by Japanese manufacturer Nikken to be used in the Play Earth Park – a campsite designed by Assemble that is at the moment under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Matter at hand founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” he continued.

“The materials react to form a fresh crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”.

Sources indicate that to show it off, Assemble constructed three miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced. The houses were named The Hut, The Tower and The Bird.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”.

The buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya remarked.

“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”.

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble noted it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Lisogorskaya stated.

“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” she continued.

SKAC recently opened two fresh gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

Recent findings suggest that building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

#206044. Industry News: How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

📅 19 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1570 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

📅 19 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.
  • It has been revealed that but as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects.
  • Sources indicate that the research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone problems, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

It has been revealed that but as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of newly introduced ones.

Sources indicate that the research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone problems, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

The lead study author said he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

Of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

First, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.).

Industry observers note that dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

Another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager indicates. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

Sources indicate that beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

Lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”.

Okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

According to recent reports, according to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager claims.

“When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall notes. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”.

Industry observers note that over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager states. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

According to recent reports, in short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager says. That said, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

It has been revealed that resistance training is vital for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall indicates. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

According to recent reports, if you’re new to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager states. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

In a recent development, protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health issues (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on crucial components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

Recent findings suggest that rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

Recent findings suggest that bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager notes. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

In a recent development, on that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager indicates. In truth, though? “The medication side effects are quite manageable when prescribed by providers who are well-versed in current practice guidelines,” she says.

Does Magnesium Help You Lose Belly Fat?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

We checked in with a doctor to find out.

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov states.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”.

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:.

Vukasinov indicates that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:.

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s crucial to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

In a recent development, remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a major hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

Staff at Edinburgh College of Art criticise "financially-driven" closure of design courses

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over one hundred staff at Edinburgh College of Art have signed an open letter addressed to the university, calling on the institution to reverse its decision to cut three craft-focussed design courses from its programme.
  • The open letter was signed by 109 unnamed staff members of Edinburgh College of Art (ECA), which confirmed on 15 September that it would stop admitting students for its undergraduate courses in jewellery and silversmithing, textiles and performance costume from 2027.
  • The move is part of a wider decision by the University of Edinburgh, which the art college merged with in 2011, to make £140 million’s worth of cuts to arts and humanities courses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photo by Colin Hattersley.

Over one hundred staff at Edinburgh College of Art have signed an open letter addressed to the university, calling on the institution to reverse its decision to cut three craft-focussed design courses from its programme.

Open letter states “deep concern”.

The open letter was signed by 109 unnamed staff members of Edinburgh College of Art (ECA), which confirmed on 15 September that it would stop admitting students for its undergraduate courses in jewellery and silversmithing, textiles and performance costume from 2027.

The move is part of a wider decision by the University of Edinburgh, which the art college merged with in 2011, to make £140 million’s worth of cuts to arts and humanities courses.

“We the undersigned are writing to mark our deep concern about the University of Edinburgh’s current financially-driven restructuring,” states the letter, which was written by an unnamed senior lecturer in the school of design and published yesterday.

“As staff who collectively provide and deliver the teaching, research, technical expertise and administration of design, we assert that there is irreparable harm being done to the core values of our subject area, school, and to the art, craft and design professions in Scotland at large,” it continues.

The open letter also asks the university to retract its decision to close the courses and requests better communication between the university and its employees.

Signatories describe an “alienating” period during which the decision to close the courses was “made without prior consultation with [the university] staff”.

“Rash decision-making based on unsubstantiated and opaque data seems to be characterising the announcements of closures and cuts, and there has been no dialogue with students and staff that can be understood as meaningful or considered consultation,” they state.

“We feel that the area’s staff have been treated callously or with very little regard by senior management, and we are writing, in part, to warn you of the damage this has created and ask you to make effort to repair it.”.

Courses part of “wider ecosystem”.

The letter goes on to emphasise the importance of “individual programmes as valuable parts of [a] wider ecosystem”, and particularly stresses the urgency of craft-based undergraduate courses in the creative sphere.

“Looking specifically at jewellery and silversmithing, textiles, and performance costume, these are subjects that teach, in different and inherently valuable ways, specialised material knowledge and sensibilities, innovative critiques, and developments of systems of production and consumption, great capacities to research-through-making, and the ability to speak to a society’s needs through aesthetic form, the power of narrative, and the arts of material, chemical and technological mastery and manipulation,” it states.

The letter is addressed to the University of Edinburgh Court, the university’s governing body, which is scheduled to meet on 7 December to review the decision.

The open letter is the most recent statement issued by a collective against the decision to cut the courses. It follows a live petition led by arts organisation Craft Scotland calling for the urgent reinstatement of “the only undergraduate craft courses offered by Edinburgh College of Art” amidst public backlash.

In response to the letter, ECA principal Juan Cruz commented, “we remain committed to the strength and distinctiveness of our disciplines, as well as to the many other making and craft-based approaches that we offer at Edinburgh College of Art”.

“These subjects will continue to be represented within the wider curriculum, supported by ECA’s specialist academic and technical expertise and facilities,” he added.

#206040. Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1703 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Upcoming York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.
  • It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including MAJOR, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.
  • Industry observers note that and yet, not everyone is a fan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Main photo by Dimitar Harizanov.

For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Upcoming York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including MAJOR, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

Industry observers note that and yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

It has been revealed that so, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

“I’m totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it’s possible,” said Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm Buro Happold. “There are a few things that I think we can’t even argue about anymore.”.

There is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings bolsters biodiversity. And, he claims, “there’s no discussion” that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can effectively keep homes cooler in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of the trees and soil, increasing the carbon cost by more than what the trees themselves will be able to sequester. Critics therefore argue that any carbon savings from reduced energy use are a red herring, because a similar benefit could be achieved through much simpler passive cooling measures such as awnings and shutters.

“I think that criticism is entirely legitimate, particularly if carbon sequestration is being used as the main justification,” stated World Green Building Council technical lead for sustainable buildings Carolina Montano Owen.

“Trees do sequester carbon, but relatively slowly compared with the upfront emissions that can arise from additional reinforced concrete or steel needed for large planters, supporting structure and associated systems.”.

Even Dutch architecture studio MVRDV, one of the most fervent incorporators of trees on buildings, admitted in its Carbon Confessions exhibition held earlier this year that it would take hundreds of years to offset the climate impact of its La Serre project in Paris, currently under construction. MVRDV declined to contribute to this article.

While the phenomenon of trees on buildings goes back hundreds of years, to the Guinigi Tower in Tuscany, the undisputed poster child for the current movement stands at the other end of Italy.

Bosco Verticale in Milan is a pair of residential high-rises covered in 21,000 plants, including 800 trees up to 20 metres tall. It caused a sensation upon its completion in 2014, and was later selected by Dezeen as that year’s most significant building in the world.

The architect behind Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri, has since delivered other “vertical forests” in Eindhoven, Huanggang, Tirana and Utrecht, with several more on the way.

Industry observers note that as you’d expect, he is bullish about the benefits of putting trees on buildings. He points to analysis by Arup, which concluded that the embodied carbon of Bosco Verticale is just one per cent greater than a comparable building with balconies of the same depth without vegetation.

“The load of the greenery, including the soil, trees and so on, really only slightly exceeds the variable loads that, in any case, must necessarily be taken into account in the structural design of cantilevered space,” he told Dezeen.

Boeri argues that changes to the construction process – such as the use of prefabrication methods or mass timber – promise to cut the embodied cost further in future vertical forest projects.

Even so, Philip Oldfield, head of the University of New South Wales’ School of Built Environment, is not convinced.

“I think the equation is pretty challenging to make the case that trees on buildings are beneficial from a greenhouse-gas emissions perspective,” he told Dezeen.

However, Oldfield points out, that’s not to say that architects adorning their buildings with trees are necessarily acting in bad faith.

“I’m a fan of Bosco Verticale,” he stated. “I think it’s a really inspiring building, but not from a carbon perspective.”.

“What inspires me about Bosco Verticale is it says, ‘hey, look: you can have a hint of suburban lifestyle in a high-rise urban building,’ which could make high-density living more attractive to a greater socio-economic spectrum, and then that may be more sustainable in the long run.”.

Though harder to measure than carbon, it’s generally acknowledged that incorporating greenery into dense urban settings has positives for human wellbeing.

For instance, when Oldfield helped to conduct a post-occupancy study of the social housing development Pinnacle@Duxton in Singapore, he witnessed children sitting under trees to do their homework 50 storeys in the sky.

“Singapore’s been able to add trees and green across its built environment, and it has fundamentally changed the experience of the city, I think for the better,” he noted.

With a very high-rise urban landscape, year-round hot weather, lots of rain and low wind speeds, Singapore is the perfect setting for buildings bearing trees, and the construction industry here has become adept at making it work.

But in other parts of the world, things have gone less successfully. Jean Nouvel’s One Central Park in Sydney, for example, had to undergo emergency repairs after one of its heavy planter boxes fell to the ground in 2022.

And in Chengdu, there were reports that barely any of the 826 apartments at Qiyi City Forest Garden were occupied a few years after its completion due to a mosquito infestation.

Even the most ardent fans of trees on buildings agree that it’s not always the right solution.

In a recent development, “I’m totally positive about it, but I think it should be taken case-by-case,” said Scherner. “There may be cases where the purpose or the objective of the project are not really realistic.”.

“If the right multidisciplinary team is not there from the start – and I’m talking about ecologists, horticulturalists, together with engineers, structural engineers, architects, landscape architects and all that – then many things can go wrong.”.

Sources indicate that “There are many flops,” stated Boeri. “If you decide to follow the approach that we have, you take several risks, so it’s very important to be aware of the risk and to run all the technical issues and tools that you need if you want to do it properly.”.

“Botany is not a superficial discipline – it’s very complex, very rich, and so when you want to realise a building where trees are acting as live subjects, you have to study a lot.”.

Bosco Verticale was subject to a huge amount of strategic planning in collaboration with botanists, from the selection and preparation of the plants, to soil chemistry, to developing systems for irrigation and maintenance.

“Flying gardeners” now scale the buildings twice a year, while thousands of ladybirds were purchased to control pests and cranes were installed on top of the towers in anticipation of removing larger dead trees. In the event, Boeri claims fewer than 15 trees have died at Bosco Verticale, and the cranes have never been required.

Sceptics’ early predictions of mass plant deaths at buildings bearing trees have, in general, not come to pass.

But concern about whether some of these buildings are more interested in making a visual statement than being ecologically responsible has lingered.

For Montano Owen, this is the crucial test of whether the approach is justified.

“The difference is whether planting is an integrated environmental strategy or primarily aesthetic,” she said.

“A poor example is essentially decorative: oversized concrete or steel planters added to achieve a ‘green’ aesthetic, substantial additional structural loads, high irrigation requirements, inappropriate species, difficult maintenance access and high tree mortality.”.

Sources indicate that boeri agrees. “I believe that what we have done works because we were not considering plants as an ornamental presence, and this is very important for me,” he mentioned. “What we are doing is really to create buildings for trees, a house for trees.”.

Among the most high-profile projects accused of using trees as mere decoration is Heatherwick Studio’s 1,000 Trees shopping centre in Shanghai, completed in 2022.

Soon after the finished building was unveiled, Oldfield criticised the design in a piece on Dezeen.

“The trees are a one-liner, contributing to a sense of urban drama, but with little substance as to how they might provide tangible benefits to the environment, or the community,” he wrote.

Subject to similar criticisms recently was MVRDV’s design for the upcoming Rotterdam Rocks!. Writing on Dezeen, architecture historian Barnabas Calder called for the project to be scrapped, saying that “putting plants on a building doesn’t make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan”.

These studios may argue – as Heatherwick Studio leader Thomas Heatherwick has previously done – that there is intrinsic value in designing buildings that capture the imagination of the public.

That in turn feeds into a broader debate about whether the priority for architecture should be to minimise up-front carbon, or maximise the chance that buildings are retained by future generations.

In any case, with the trees-on-buildings trend showing little sign of abating, Montano Owen has a checklist for architects taking up the approach.

“Start with the local context and environmental needs,” she said. “Choose species that are suited to the location. Minimise extra structure, materials and loads. Consider water and maintenance needs from the start. Plan for vegetation to survive, grow and mature long term. Avoid solutions that need heavy structures, intensive irrigation or frequent plant replacement for limited environmental benefit.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The key question is this,” she added. “Is this the best place and most resource-efficient way to achieve the environmental benefits we want? Sometimes trees on buildings could make sense. In most cases, trees at street or ground level may provide greater benefits with fewer resources.”.

Main photo by Dimitar Harizanov.

#206038. Breaking: For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

📅 20 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1718 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

📅 20 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends.
  • “I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF.
  • So she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends. Over the course of six months, they watched as she shed 30 pounds, going from 130 back to what she calls her “healthy original weight” of 100 pounds. Even still, her loved ones worried about the extent of her weight loss and didn’t want her to lose even more.

“I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF. The 34-year-old, who lives in Montreal, asked to use only her first name to protect her privacy. “I was really tired of trying.” At five feet four inches, she wasn’t obese and didn’t think her primary doctor would approve a prescription.

So she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed. Immediately after starting Wegovy, she indicates, “the weight started coming off incredibly fast.” After six months she decided she wanted to stop. But as soon as she got off Wegovy, the weight came back: She gained 10 pounds in a month. “I realized, I can’t stop,” Caroline says.

In a recent development, so for the past six months, she has been taking Wegovy again, this time at a maintenance-level dosage. But there’s one substantial difference: This time, she’s keeping it a secret from her boyfriend and family. “Now that we’re talking about kids, he’s seen all the impacts [of the drug] and he’s done with it,” she states. Since she lives alone, hiding her medication from him is relatively easy—she stashes it in the back of the fridge, since it needs to be kept cold. But she’s still worried he’ll see it, and when they travel together, she has to hide the medication in the hotel room fridge—or, if they’re visiting his parents, in their refrigerator. “So imagine, I’m hiding stuff in my parents-in-laws’ fridge, hoping they won’t see them,” she says. “It’s super awkward.”.

Recent findings suggest that caroline isn’t the only woman going to great lengths to keep her GLP-1 use a secret. On a recent thread on the r/GLP1microdosing subreddit, women shared their tips and tricks for hiding medication from their partners. One stashes them in a tomato paste box. Another uses a play food container from a child’s pretend kitchen. Still others have turned to an opaque feta cheese container, butter stick box, anchovy paste box, empty bottles of women’s probiotics and Alani Nu supplements, a plastic to-go container, a metal water bottle, a box of wine, and a baking soda box in the back of the fridge—all to conceal the weight loss medication.

“It’s a real thing,” Kia Mitchell, MD, who specializes in family and obesity medicine, tells SELF. She has seen numerous women in her Jacksonville, Florida, practice go to similar efforts to hide their medication from their partners. The first time she heard about this pattern, it was from a patient who “just didn’t want to turn this into a debate at home,” she says. “She just wanted to have the option” to take the medication. “A lot of my patients are similar,” Dr. Mitchell adds. “There’s this loss of control with the gaining of the weight, but being able to control the narrative around weight loss has been empowering and exciting” for her patients. “Because now they can reveal it on their own terms. That’s where the control comes back.”.

In a recent development, the reasons women want to reveal their weight loss medications on their own terms are palpable in that subreddit thread. “If my husband found out, it would just be a series of lectures,” wrote a user called Vivid-Act-6442. “Just don’t want to hear any negative or critical opinions,” wrote another user called [deleted]. “After 52 years of marriage, one knows one’s mate.” One woman chimed in to say she was hiding her meds from her teens—because she didn’t want them telling her ex-husband. “I just don’t feel like the questions,” she wrote.

It has been revealed that dr. Mitchell has mixed feelings about this type of secrecy. Anyone on a health journey benefits from having a “network that’s really cheering for you,” Dr. Mitchell says. “Dealing with something like this, I want people to have community.” But, she continues, it’s “empowering and protective” for women to get to decide who knows about their weight loss drugs—even if, ideally, “you really want to be in a relationship with someone you trust completely.”.

From a medical standpoint, there are some potential pitfalls to hiding GLP-1s from a significant other. For one, it’s easier to get pregnant while taking them—Mitchell states she has “several GLP-1 babies” in her practice. There are also the drugs’ potential side effects, and hiding medication can make it more difficult for a patient to turn to her partner if she’s struggling. And more generally, secrecy can cause stress. “When someone is trying to lose weight, we want their stress hormones to be as low as possible,” Dr. Mitchell says. “If you’re trying to hide [medication], we’ll be fighting an uphill battle if you’re stressed about that.”.

The bigger matter is hiding GLP-1 medications from your regular doctor, something that has become much easier thanks to the rise in telehealth companies like Hers and Ro. That’s a problem Caroline is having: She didn’t tell her doctor both times she went on Wegovy and still doesn’t want to, even though she’s concerned about how the drug may interact with the Accutane and Ritalin she takes. The idea of admitting her GLP-1 use to her doctor makes her anxious, since she doesn’t want to break their trust. But her annual physical is coming up, and her doctor will see that she’s lost a lot of weight.

“I use ChatGPT as my doctor at this point since I can’t be honest with my own doctor,” she says. “I say, ‘Hey, this is my actual weight, what type of dosage is okay to take with other drugs?’” Admittedly, she adds, this is “probably not the best option.”.

Caroline got her Wegovy prescription through Hers. During the process she was only asked for basic bloodwork and received no counseling, just “documentation to read.”.

Craig Primack, MD, the head of weight loss at Hers, tells SELF that the manufacturer’s prescribing doctors “do ask [patients] to talk with their primary care doctor about the care they’re getting.” He acknowledges that the company doesn’t do much in the way of direct counseling but says that “we ask about mental health and anxiety and stresses.” The Hers app contains what Primack terms “psychologist-built information” about topics such as sleep management and eating personas.

Dr. Primack is “absolutely” aware that some patients hide their medication from their partners. He states that some don’t want to say anything until they’ve proven they can lose weight; some don’t want to say anything because of the medication’s cost; some worry about how it could change the way they and their partner see each other. “Your weight and persona set up a dynamic in your couple,” Dr. Primack says. “When you start changing that, sometimes spouses get very jealous—‘Oh my god, you’re becoming potentially more attractive.’ Not that weight is directly linked to that, but that’s what I hear them say.”.

And then, of course, there’s the more general stigma associated with weight and weight loss. “One benefit of telemedicine is it takes the bias and stigma away,” Dr. Primack claims. “One reason we are here is because people are uncomfortable going to talk to their primary care doctor about it.”.

Whether or not Caroline decides to tell her doctor about her medication, she still will have to grapple with the larger issues that her Wegovy use, and her secrecy around it, have raised. “It’s very stressful,” she says. “The fact that not only can I not talk about it, but I’m also unable to get off of it. I don’t love the idea of taking medicine like that forever, but I’m kind of stuck with it.” She doesn’t want to gain weight, she explains. “But I wonder to which extent I’m too harsh with my criticism of my body. Maybe my goals are too intense.”.

Given the incredible degree of vulnerability and sensitivity tied up with weight loss, the dilemma about whether to tell people about a GLP-1 medication is all too understandable. But how to tell people can make it easier, states Rachel Goldman, PhD, a clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a clinical psychologist whose areas of expertise include weight management and disordered eating, tells SELF. “Framing it around their own experience and needs can make the conversation feel more manageable and less like something they have to defend,” she says.

According to recent reports, since deciding whether to have this conversation isn’t easy, Dr. Goldman would first encourage a patient to “think about their why,” she claims. “What led them to this decision? What does this treatment mean for their health and wellbeing?” Once someone feels more grounded and confident in their reasoning, “it becomes easier to communicate it with that confidence.”.

Dr. Goldman also suggests coming up with some sample scripts before having the conversation. “I would suggest that they lead with their own personal experience and not think about others and why/how others are using it,” she indicates. “I would encourage them to use ‘I’ statements.”.

It’s also helpful to think ahead of time about a partner’s potential reaction and to have a plan in place for different scenarios. Thinking about what you want from a partner is likewise helpful—is it support, understanding, “or simply space to make their own health decisions without judgement?” Dr. Goldman asks. She adds that it’s important to remember that a partner’s initial reaction might not be their final reaction—it can take time for someone to process a conversation and to work through their own biases and misconceptions.

“Ultimately,” she indicates, “the goal isn’t to have a perfect conversation, but it’s to open the door to more honesty, connection, and support over time.”.

But if that fails, there’s always a box of anchovy paste.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (503 w)

Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging designer of the year Simon Skinner

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Peter Hansen unless stated.
  • In a recent development, this year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards.
  • Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Peter Hansen unless stated.

In a recent development, this year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

“My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life,” Skinner told Dezeen.

“What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer new perspectives on things we know and take for granted.”.

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also “the same things that make me suffer”.

“You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty,” he said.

“A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work.”.

Over the coming year, along with creating latest collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

“I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead,” he said.

It has been revealed that “When I started researching Afro combs at Konstfack, I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work,” he continued.

“I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited and what happens when you change their material, scale or context.”.

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning Skinner, as described by the designer:.

“An ongoing project in which vintage glass sourced from flea markets and second-hand shops is brought together in sculptural lighting compositions.

“Drawing on the memories and associations embedded in these found objects, the work explores the relationship between material, memory and light.”.

“Crafted in my studio, these combs celebrate rituals and traditions surrounding textured hair.

“Informed by historical references and personal experiences, they reimagine an everyday object through distinctive forms and symbols.”.

“Extending the exploration of beauty rituals within the Syntax collection, the Vanity Table offers an alternative reading of an object associated with personal grooming.”.

“These one-of-a-kind pieces, a daybed and an armchair, are upholstered in hand-dyed canvas in deep magenta hues.

“Combining traditional upholstery techniques with an experimental approach to colour and detail, the pieces embrace the irregularities of the dyeing process, making them an integral part of their character.”.

Sources indicate that “This piece of furniture explores our relationship to the mechanical lock. The lock is integrated into the leg, with keys used to secure the connection between the leg and the seat.

“The keys can also serve as hooks for keychains and personal belongings, inviting individual expression.”.
