  • That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.
  • Industry observers note that though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD.

That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.

Industry observers note that though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat. Prescription rates were still very low, and it seemed like no one actually knew anyone who was taking it.

Sources indicate that now, in 2026, over 1 in 10 US adults are taking a GLP-1 medication. Most of us know someone on it (or we’re on it ourselves).

With wider use, opinions towards the medication have softened too. Most coaches no longer see it as a threat, and instead appreciate it as a valuable tool for certain clients, with coaching as an additive complement.

According to recent reports, many coaches still have concerns though, primarily about their clients’ long term health on the medication. (Among the worries: Loss of muscle mass! Using a “band-aid” solution! Bypassing foundational health habits! And more!).

However, whether you count yourself as a GLP-1 supporter or a GLP-1 skeptic, there’s a framing that might change the way you think about your work in this field:.

As Kate Solovieva, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Community, indicates: “As a coach, you’re not in the GLP-1 world; you’re in the GLP-1 support world.”.

That’s actually good news. Because trying to coach everyone taking a GLP-1 just isn’t possible. And spending time thinking about all the people using GLP-1s “the wrong way” is, bluntly, wasted energy. Some of those people just don’t want, need, or aren’t ready for your help.

Meanwhile, there is a subgroup of people on GLP-1s who are ready, willing, and able to receive your support. Honing in on this group is where you can actually make a difference (and where your business can thrive).

In the following article, we’ll cover seven GLP-1 clients you’re likely to meet. Each reflects a different point in the GLP-1 medication journey, and a different level of readiness for coaching. Based on our experience coaching over 175,000 clients (of which an increasing number are on GLP-1s), we’ll offer strategies to work with each.

Before we begin, a reminder: People change, and readiness isn’t fixed.

A person who starts off saying “I’m doing fine on my own” may eventually morph into “I’m flailing and really need someone else in my corner”—and vice versa.

If the person in front of you sounds like one of these clients, that’s where they are right now. So listen carefully to how your client speaks at every session, and respond dynamically.

In general, Coach Kate says someone is usually ready for coaching when they demonstrate two things:.

Keep that in the back of your mind as you interact with client prospects, and as you read about each client, summarized in the table below.

Now, on to the different GLP-1 clients.

This is the person who’s started a GLP-1 medication—and they love it.

They’ve experienced minimal side effects, and have gotten great results on a relatively low dose.

They haven’t changed much about their exercise habits or their diet (except the eating less part, which the medication has taken care of), but they’re seeing what they want to see on the scale, so they don’t feel motivated to change anything.

It might be tempting to “lure” this kind of client in by warning them of the dangers of using a GLP-1 medication without adding in long-term health behaviors (like resistance training and strategic nutrition), but this type of approach can backfire.

Industry observers note that at best, you may sound like a downer. At worst, you may sound like an active antagonist.

In a recent development, in Motivational Interviewing, a communication approach commonly used in coaching, this is called the “righting reflex.” It’s the urge that coaches, counselors, and therapists often have to help or “correct course” for their client. You see them doing something “wrong,” and you want to help them “fix” it.

However, following this instinct may actually strengthen a client’s defenses, and prevent change.

If a person is flying high on their current approach, their readiness for coaching is extremely low.

As Coach Kate says, “they’re just not my person yet.”.

Your best move with this client is to genuinely celebrate their current results, then plant the seed for support should they need it in the future.

For example, you could say: “It must feel so good to see all these positive results! If you ever feel like you want to work on another layer, like resistance training or optimizing your nutrition, I’d love to work together.”.

It has been revealed that then, just stay available. (“My door is always open!”).

This is the person who hasn’t started a GLP-1 medication—and might never, despite being a great candidate for one.

Maybe their doctor has already suggested the medication to them and they’ve read everything they can on the topic.

In a recent development, and yet, they’re frozen with fear at the starting line. They’re afraid of side effects, of being on medication for life, of not holding up their end of the bargain. (“I’ve been trying to start strength training for years. If I take this medication it matters even more… What if I still can’t do it?”).

Toni Bauer, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Coaching and Education Operations also says that, in some cases, a client’s hesitation isn’t about side effects. “Some of our clients wonder, ‘Am I a good person or a bad person if I start taking a GLP-1 medication? Am I weak? Am I giving up?’” Coach Toni says these concerns aren’t unique to GLP-1 medications, but they seem to be especially common.

Industry observers note that she reasons, “If you have high cholesterol, are you weak for taking cholesterol medication? No. But often people don’t view obesity as a disease at a societal level, so the conversation is different here.”.

Regardless of the root cause of this person’s hesitation, the advice below can help them find clarity.

First, let’s be clear: Deciding whether or not to take a medication isn’t a coaching decision, and falls out of your scope of practice. That choice is ultimately up to your client and a medical provider who can assess whether a GLP-1 is appropriate given their medical history.

That stated, clients may still come to you wanting to discuss their options.

So the question becomes: How do you support someone through a decision you can’t make for them?

Industry observers note that coach Toni advises: “You can share facts and data. For example, study results and what you’ve seen with other clients. But you can’t say, ‘For you, this is the right choice.’”.

Instead, the biggest coaching opportunity here is to help clients articulate what’s actually driving their hesitation.

This hesitation about whether to do something different or stay the same is called ambivalence, and it’s a normal (albeit uncomfortable) stage of change.

It has been revealed that problem is, without the right tools, a person can stay stuck in ambivalence for months or even years. And, much like being stuck at an airport in between two destinations, it sucks.

In a recent development, but at PN, we have a cool exercise to deal with client ambivalence. It’s called the 4 Crazy Questions. Essentially, you explore:.

In this context, the questions can help a client explore the risk of starting a GLP-1 (which they’ve probably already voiced), but also the risk of not starting, which they may not have considered yet.

Our 4 Crazy Questions worksheet can encourage clients to explore the pros and cons of both choices. With these considerations laid out explicitly, most people feel a lot more clear about their next steps—or at least what questions they need to ask their medical provider before they can move forward.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, this exercise doesn’t have a “right” outcome. Some people work through it and fill the prescription. Others decide the medication isn’t for them, and that’s fine. (It’s also worth reminding clients that starting isn’t necessarily permanent: With their provider’s input, a trial run on the medication is a perfectly valid way in.).

Sources indicate that either way, there are opportunities to support your client. As Coach Toni puts it: “Whether you go ‘natural’ or whether you go GLP-1, the foundational habits are essentially the same.”.

This is the person who started a GLP-1 with lots of optimism—and now feels like they have a plague that won’t end.

According to recent reports, in a cruel twist, this person might actually be seeing great fat loss results. And yet, they’re nauseated, exhausted, dreading their next dose, and wondering whether it’s worth continuing this medication.

Sources indicate that adding to their sense of defeat, they may also be comparing themselves to a “Honeymooner” in their life, so they might also be wondering if there’s something wrong with them. (“It worked so well for my friend! I must be broken in some way.”).

First, offer some neutral education to depersonalize their experience.

Namely, they should know that side effects are extremely common: About half of users report nausea, a third report diarrhea, and a fifth report vomiting.1 So, what this person thinks is exceptional might actually just be a normal adjustment. (This doesn’t make the experience suck less, but it can give them some hope.).

Also, getting GLP-1s right is a process of trial and error: the right medication, the right dose, and the right nutritional strategies to reduce symptoms.

Sources indicate that if their symptoms are severe, get them to loop in their doctor. Medication type and dosing is under the purview of a medical professional, so involving them is essential.

After that, your best coaching move is to suggest an experiment.

Recent findings suggest that ▶ Ask about dose. To be clear, you’re asking about it, not adjusting it. States Coach Toni: “Often, when people are experiencing extreme side effects, they’ve ratcheted up their dose too quickly. Sometimes the easiest way to keep somebody on a GLP-1 who’s experiencing high side effects is to lower their dosage.” Coach Toni makes clear that while dosage isn’t a coach’s domain, you can help draw a client’s attention to it.

Recent findings suggest that ▶ Start a food journal. It doesn’t need to be every day—just around the meals that precede the worst symptoms. You’re looking for three things:.

▶ Try smaller portions, eaten more often. Coach Toni notes if you only try one thing, this one is the most reliable strategy. GLP-1 clients may be tempted to cut meals when symptoms are high, but this increases the likelihood of undereating and nutrient deficiencies. The goal, in her words: “Can we get small enough, frequent enough meals that we get nutrients in, but they never feel overwhelmed or super full?”.

To stay within your scope of practice, language matters.

Don’t say: “You’re nauseous, so you should eat smaller meals.”.

Industry observers note that instead, say: “Folks who are nauseous sometimes do better with smaller, more frequent meals. Want to try it this week and see what you notice?”.

In a recent development, in the first example, you’ve offered a “prescription” (which coaches can’t legally do). In the second example, you’ve offered an experiment to consider.

Side effects (such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and/or diarrhea) are extremely common among GLP-1 users, and typically last one to two weeks after initiating the medication. Some symptoms can last longer (particularly constipation), but most are mild to moderate, and usually improve within a few weeks.

Symptoms can also return each time a dosage is increased, though they’re usually milder and more short-lived. These too tend to improve after the first week or so.

However, you should strongly encourage a client to reach out promptly to their medical provider if they notice:.

Sources indicate that reassure your client they’re not being dramatic by reporting these symptoms. Their medical team needs to hear this kind of information to help them get the best results, while preserving overall health.

It has been revealed that also: Your client will get better care if they show up prepared. So, get them to jot down and bring:.

This is the person whose results look great, but less visible changes are creating longer term risks.

This person is likely to be quite sedentary, and when you ask what they do for exercise, they might tell you “I walk.” But they’re not the outlier kind of walker who consistently gets 20,000 steps a day. They just… walk a little.

Women are more likely to fall into this category, especially if they come from a generation or culture where strength training simply wasn’t a thing women did (or were welcomed to do).

Additionally, this person might be running on a decades-long plain-toast-and-coffee breakfast habit, with lower protein intake already ingrained before medication further reduced appetite.

In a recent development, the scale is dropping though, so they’re thrilled. It’s just that nobody’s measuring what kind of weight is dropping.

Keep in mind that this description is a starting hypothesis, not a diagnosis. Low activity and low protein raise the risk of muscle loss, but they don’t confirm it. That’s what the measures below are for.

Your job is to bring awareness to the invisible. Because once this person sees what’s at stake, they’ll be more likely to see the value in changing their habits, and in coaching.

However, theoretical warnings about muscle loss are easy to dismiss.

This is one of the reasons why Coach Kate indicates, “I don’t care if I coach you or not—please just get a DEXA as a baseline.”.

When a person has a quantifiable, objective measure of their muscle composition, it’s often more motivating than any amount of abstract concern.

Ideally, every person who begins a GLP-1 medication should get a DEXA scan before they start, then again at six or twelve months to see how they’re progressing.

If a client can’t or won’t do a DEXA, assess strength and function in other ways. Ask: “How do the stairs feel compared to a few months ago? What about carrying groceries?” Gather objective data too, recording baselines for squat, deadlift, and bench press (or other accessible exercises) to compare to over time. Declines in any of these areas can reveal potential muscle loss, and can motivate a client to take action.

Without protective strategies, up to 40 percent of weight lost from GLP-1 medications can come from lean mass, with a majority of that being muscle.2.

In order to prevent that from happening, there are two behaviors to prioritize:.

▶ Protein at every meal. When appetite is suppressed, every bite has to earn its place. Aim for 25-40 grams of protein at every meal and 15-20 grams for snacks. (On days when appetite is severely suppressed, protein powders can be a more palatable way to reach that target.).

Sources indicate that ▶ Strength training, scaled to what they’d actually do. The term “weight lifting” might overwhelm a person who’s never set foot in a gym, so don’t start there. Start where PN always starts: Ask what they could do twice this week that they’re 9-out-of-10 confident they’d actually do. Sit-to-stands off the couch. A few moves with a resistance band. Bodyweight anything. Scale up from there, one week at a time.

This is the person for whom the medication has worked a little too well.

Their appetite hasn’t just decreased—it’s gone.

It has been revealed that they’re not eating enough, and often don’t notice until you ask. “When did you last eat?” you say, and they say, “Ummm… Yesterday afternoon? I think?”.

Their protein and overall calorie intake is plummeting, and soon their energy levels will too.

Plus, something more subtle might also be happening: Food stops being a pleasure and becomes a chore, or even a source of dread.

Industry observers note that for some, this might seem like an upside down world. They may have spent their whole life fighting to eat less. The idea of fighting to eat more feels completely absurd—and entirely off their radar.

Before anything else: If there’s an active eating disorder in the picture, this medication likely shouldn’t have been prescribed. A vulnerability to disordered eating can both contribute to or be triggered by the above scenario.

According to recent reports, so, scope of practice first. Ask this person if they’ve ever struggled with disordered eating. If the answer is yes, refer out to a doctor or a dietitian. You can absolutely stay involved as a guide, but not as the only professional in the room. Have your referral network ready before you need it.

Sources indicate that but sometimes, you won’t know. Your client may have been screened and cleared. Or, they may not have disclosed. So your job is to figure out what you’re actually looking at—and that starts with what Coach Toni calls the “show me” approach.

It has been revealed that as with every client here, treat this one as something to investigate, not a label. Rather than acting on a hunch, collect something concrete, such as a few days of food logging (in writing or via photos).

From there, it branches two ways.

▶ If they’ll track, do some food math, and the numbers may do the work for you. When some clients see that their calorie intake is hovering around 800 to 1,000 Calories per day, it’s the only wake up call they need. They weren’t intentionally restricting; they genuinely just had no idea.

For this client, establishing an eating routine is the best next action.

Sources indicate that your client may be used to following appetite as a cue to eat, but now that medication has removed it, they need a different cue. That means eating on a schedule, likely every 3–4 hours, including protein at every one of those occasions. Portions can be small if appetite is very low, but they should be nutrient-dense.

▶ If they won’t track—and especially if they resist in a way that feels purposely avoidant—that resistance itself is information.

Coach Toni suggests that if you suspect that disordered eating is in the picture and a client is really resistant about tracking, it might be time for a crucial conversation—an often uncomfortable, but honest and essential conversation between a client and a coach.

In a recent development, she suggests leading with non-judgement and safety. For example:.

Industry observers note that “I want you to know this is a safe space to talk. My goal as a coach is always to prioritize your overall health. However, there have been a couple of things you’ve shared recently that have me wondering whether we’re protecting your body’s basic needs.”.

Then name the specific things you noticed, sticking to facts. (“You’ve mentioned you’ve been losing hair and struggling more during workouts. Those can both be signs of undereating. Would you be open to revisiting food journaling for a short stretch so we can see more clearly what’s happening, or telling your doctor about your symptoms?”).

If this conversation is enough to help a client see the value in tracking, follow the advice after “If they’ll track” above.

If what surfaces is a genuinely troubled relationship with food, refer out, while offering to stay involved for support as needed.

This is the person who got the results they wanted with the medication, and is now choosing to wean off.

They’re not quitting because of crappy results or intolerable side effects, they’ve simply decided they don’t want to be on a GLP-1 forever.

The coaching opportunity here is, in part, about tempering expectations.

Recent findings suggest that most people imagine coming off as the finish line. Instead though, it’s more like starting a different endurance course: The medication has been managing their appetite, and now they have to.

Ideally, you start working with this client while the medication is still doing some of the heavy lifting with appetite regulation. If you can have six months to build the right habits as well as prepare mentally for the tapering off period, your client will be in a much better position.

In a recent development, make sure the previously mentioned habits—like resistance training and optimizing protein—are already firmly established. If your client is managing those habits consistently (not perfectly, but consistently), even on their busiest, most stressful, most side-effect-disrupted days, then they’re more likely to be able to maintain them when they’re off their medication and food distractions re-enter the picture.

After that, work on how you’ll continue to define success. This client has been accustomed to measuring it on the scale, but the scale will move—some regain is normal. So, ask them early: What does success look like if the scale ticks up eight pounds but your habits hold?

Industry observers note that be honest about the odds, too. People who changed nothing while on the medication almost universally regain most of the weight—usually within the first year and a half or so3—because the appetite that went down comes right back up.

However, people who integrate and sustain healthier nutrition and exercise behaviors while they’re on medication are four times better at maintaining a ten percent or higher weight loss when they come off the medication.4.

This is the person who was also getting great results on the medication—except instead of choosing to go off it on their own time, they’re forced to quit due to external circumstances.

Maybe their insurance stopped covering it, or they lost the job that came with the benefits, or the one drug they tolerated turned out to cost four times as much as the one they couldn’t tolerate.

About 50 percent of GLP-1 users stop the medication within the first year of using it.5 Some stop due to side effects, and others stop because they’ve gotten the results they want and they want to see if they can maintain them drug-free. But many are simply priced out. The latter is an especially frustrating scenario because, for this person, a “solution” exists. It’s just that, for them, the solution is out of reach.

Sources indicate that understandably, this person may be angry or even ashamed that they can’t afford this medication. Those feelings may or may not show up in your coaching, but it’s good to prepare for them anyway.

First, reassure this person that this is a system failure, not a personal one.

It has been revealed that whether someone can access affordable medication comes down to their insurance strategy, the region they live in, and their socioeconomic status—also known as the social determinants of health. Those forces shape health outcomes far more than willpower does, and none of them are a measure of how hard someone has tried or how “worthy” they are.

Acknowledging that reality isn’t about throwing up your hands and saying, “Well, I’m screwed!” Rather, it’s about accepting some miserable truths about the world, and then shifting from self-blame to problem-solving.

Once they’ve had a chance to process some (very valid) anger and disappointment, it’s time to focus on what they can control.

At PN, we call this the Spheres of Control exercise. The image below reveals you how it works.

Access, price, and coverage are not on the list of controllables, and fighting those realities may only compound frustration.

Meanwhile, they can control other influential factors, like their protein intake, their training, their sleep, their food environment, and maybe their next insurance appeal.

Use the image above to begin a conversation with your client about what is within their control, and lean in hard on those factors.

Sources indicate that the truth is, you can’t predict how a client will respond to medication. And, some regain after stopping it is expected.

However, diet and lifestyle habits hugely affect what kind of weight clients lose, plus the rate and amount of that regain.

It has been revealed that “I can’t promise anyone they’ll lose a specific amount of weight or that they’ll never regain it—and I’d be suspicious of any coach who did. What I can tell you is that the habits we build while the medication is doing its work are the ones that’ll still stand when it isn’t.”.

Of course, “coming off” isn’t the endpoint for everyone. Many providers now treat obesity as a chronic condition and these medications as long-term therapy—the same way we’d treat cardiac disease. Again, whether someone stays on, tapers, or stops is a conversation for them and their provider.

Recent findings suggest that but for those who do come off, Coach Toni claims the people who hold their results share one thing: “They maintain consistency with their behaviors as if they were still on the medication. Like nothing changes.”.

She shares an analogy for why that works:.

“Think about the Oregon Trail. Wagon wheels made ruts in the trail by hitting the same ground over and over and over. You can still see those ruts today. Habits are the same way: If you lay down those neural pathways and reinforce them enough times while your client is on the medication, they’ll have a better chance of continuing on the same path even when they go off the medication.”.

It’s not: “You’ll keep it off.”.

It’s: “While the medication is doing its work, we’ll cut ruts deep enough that those pathways will still be there after the medication is gone.”.

Practically, that means regular resistance training, rock solid nutrition, appetite awareness, and attending to the parts of health that never show up on a scale—sleep, energy, mood, relationships, and identity, which is where Coach Toni lands:.

“Ideally, your client will have embraced the identity of a ‘new person.’ As in, ‘I am the person who wakes up at 6 a.m. and walks two miles. I am the person who eats protein at every meal. I am the person who does resistance training because it builds the tissue I need to age well.’ That’s the client who maintains.”.

The seven client examples above help you answer two questions:.

Is this person ready for coaching?

How do I meet them where they are?

Once someone becomes your client, the question changes to:.

And when nausea, fatigue, stalled results, and weakening strength and physical function all show up at once in the same client, that can be tricky to answer.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Sources indicate that most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Sources indicate that off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Industry observers note that marriott Bonvoy® is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One key structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Sources indicate that finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

It has been revealed that search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:.

In a recent development, most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

It has been revealed that now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

Sources indicate that for a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

In a recent development, do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Sources indicate that do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Industry observers note that avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Recent findings suggest that avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it demonstrates Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. 15-Minute Evening Yoga to Unwind (That You Can Practice in Bed)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this short evening yoga routine is designed to help you release stress when you’re ready to wind down for the evening or let go of the day.
  • Recent findings suggest that the stretches are essentially yin yoga poses, except we’re staying in the shapes for less time than the usual 3 to 5 minutes that we expect from yin yoga.
  • Because you’re trying to calm the body and mind, these stretches are not about chasing sensation or pushing yourself into an extreme shape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this short evening yoga routine is designed to help you release stress when you’re ready to wind down for the evening or let go of the day. It brings you a full-body stretch and a lot of relaxation. The poses are all either seated or lying down, so there’s very little effort required. You can even practice the yoga for better sleep routine in bed.

Recent findings suggest that the stretches are essentially yin yoga poses, except we’re staying in the shapes for less time than the usual 3 to 5 minutes that we expect from yin yoga. But these are all poses that you would find in a yin yoga class, so you could stay in any or all of the poses a little longer. The exact 15-minute sequence could be a 75-minute yin yoga class if you have the time or wake up in the middle of the night and are trying to go back to sleep.

Because you’re trying to calm the body and mind, these stretches are not about chasing sensation or pushing yourself into an extreme shape. Try to find a little more ease in each pose as you invite a slower, deeper rhythm to your breath, which signals your nervous system that it’s time to unwind and release. Every time you exhale, see if you can relax a different part of your body and let go of whatever is on your mind from your day.

It has been revealed that these stretches are suitable for any experience level. No props are required. Let yourself linger and release into each shape and stay there for 5 to 10 breaths.

Start sitting and then straighten your right leg in front of you. Option one, you can either do your Head to Knee Pose, which we call Half Butterfly in yin yoga, with your left foot to the inside of your thigh.

Option two, you can stretch a little more through the hip and inner thigh if you take your left knee out to the side and your foot behind you with your heel tucked in toward your glutes. If you try option two and you experience any pain or sensitivity in the knee, come back to the first option.

It has been revealed that then start to walk your hands in front of in a forward bend. Let it be a passive stretch, which means you want to let your back round and your head hang. Let gravity do the work for you. Stay here for about 5 breaths or so. While you are in the pose, can you let go of any tension in your arms, jaw, and neck?

Press your hands against the mat and slowly lift yourself back up to sitting.

Industry observers note that if it’s not already, bend your left knee out to the side so it’s in line with your left hip. You want to create about a 90-degree bend in your leg and bring your ankle in line with your knee. Then align your right knee so it’s also at a 90-degree angle.

Press your left hip back toward the wall behind you and start to walk your hands back on a diagonal behind you. As soon as you start to feel that sensation through your left hip, pause and breathe into it a little. You can stay propped up on your palms, lower onto your forearms, or lie all the way flat on your back. I’m going to stay propped up on my hands. I find I get the best stretch this way. Breathe here.

Walk your hands in, slowly lifting yourself upright.

Industry observers note that bring your left leg straight in front of you. Cross your left foot over your right thigh, bringing your left foot to the mat outside your right leg. Wrap your right arm around your left and bring your left fingertips to the mat behind you and let them support you. Lift tall through the spine, pressing your shoulders down and away from your ears, then twist toward the left in a Seated Twist. Press into your left big toe and keep both sit bones on the mat. Breathe here.

Then take your Head to Knee or Half Butterfly on the other side, followed by Deer Pose or 90/90 and Seated Twist.

Lower all the way down onto your back. Pull your knees toward your chest. Then initiate a little pumping motion. So place your hands on the tops of your knees.

As you inhale, straighten your arms and push your thighs away.

In a recent development, as you exhale, draw your thighs back toward you. Try to relax your legs fully so your arms are controlling the motion. As you do this simple motion, you’re trying to release your lower back muscles as much as possible. You almost want to feel like your legs are moving in water. Take a few more like this.

The next time you bring your knees toward you, widen them toward your shoulders. Either hold here or come into Happy Baby by grabbing hold of your big toes with your two peace fingers, taking your elbows to the insides of your knees, and using your arms to push your legs open a little more. Think of pressing your lower back into the mat, keeping your head and shoulders down on the ground. Sometimes rocking a little side to side can feel really good.

Industry observers note that from Happy Baby, keep your right knee close to your chest and extend your left leg straight on the mat to stretch the hip flexors along the front of your left hip. You can take a few ankle rolls with your right foot by making circles, flexing and pointing through your toes, and making any motion through the ankles. Reverse the direction of those circles.

Industry observers note that come into your twist from here, crossing your right leg over your body to the left with the help of your left hand. Stretch your right arm straight out to the side. Think of relaxing your right shoulder down and trying to stack your right hip on top of your left hip.

Recent findings suggest that if you notice yourself obsessing over anything or going over and over a particular thought, just observe what’s happening. Notice that tendency in that pattern, and maybe instead focus on something else that’s a bit more tangible, like the physical sensations in your body from the poses or just the flow of your breath.

Come all the way back to center.

In a recent development, straighten your right leg any amount, stretching the hamstrings. You can flex and point your foot a couple times.

Recent findings suggest that then come into Reclined Pigeon Pose by sliding your left foot in, crossing your right ankle over the top of your left knee in a figure-four shape, and reaching your arms along either side of your left leg as you pull your left thigh toward you. Only using a little arm strength. Try to relax your shoulders and keep your head on the  mat. Breathe here.

Keep your left knee drawn toward your chest as you release the pose and extend your right leg straight on the mat. Repeat your ankle rolls, Reclined Twist, and Reclined Pigeon on your left side.

According to recent reports, then you’ll set yourself up for Savasana, your final resting pose. Take up some space with your arms and your legs and then close your eyes. You might do a body scan, bringing your awareness to the crown of your head and slowly working your way down to your fingers and your toes, asking each muscle to relax, to let go, almost as if you could sink into the mat or mattress.

Allow yourself about two minutes here or more if you have the time. Just enjoy the silence and stillness. If you’re already in bed, maybe you stay here.

Start to deepen your breath. Maybe you move your fingers and toes a little. Nice and slow, roll to one side and come to take a seat. Find some length in your spine as you release your shoulders down.

Just pause here. Notice how you feel after just a few minutes of stretching and silence.

Thank you so much, everyone, for doing this short bedtime practice. I hope you feel ready to ease into the rest of your night.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN).

Industry observers note that one month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

Florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

However, ahead of Kona, Ditlev stated he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

Ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

It has been revealed that by the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

In a recent development, ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

According to recent reports, hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

I’m working my way through all of them.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, remarked it this way:.

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Of course that’s going to feel rough!

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:.

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

After multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

According to recent reports, and it’s important to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

According to recent reports, you know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Industry observers note that instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

It has been revealed that maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Industry observers note that try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌.

Sources indicate that and if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

If you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

Your on-ramp doesn’t have to be forever.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

#205955. Tech Report: The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

Tech Report: The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.
  • It has been revealed that the righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change.
  • Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.

It has been revealed that the righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

We are now entering upside-down-land.

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

In a recent development, push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

It has been revealed that instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!).

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:.

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

Here’s what Coach Jeremy has to say:.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Industry observers note that not long after, another friend highlighted up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:.

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”.

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really major stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

Sources indicate that with over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

Here’s what Coach Kate has to say:.

According to recent reports, you know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

And that is not the case at all.

Industry observers note that at least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

Recent findings suggest that but weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

In a recent development, this realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

It has been revealed that I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the substantial goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

Industry observers note that but striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

In a recent development, health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Here’s what Coach Azul has to say:.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”.

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

Industry observers note that I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

Industry observers note that I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

In a recent development, because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”).

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try newly introduced things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

Industry observers note that with over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

Here’s what Coach Dom has to say:.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most notable thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’.

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My fresh definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”.

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

It has been revealed that then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”.

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

According to recent reports, it turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

Recent findings suggest that with over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

Here’s what Coach Jason has to say:.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”.

It has been revealed that he was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

Recent findings suggest that in his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

Sources indicate that that client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.).

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

#205954. What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (975 w)
📖 Baca

What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that who holds the Ironman world record?
  • After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.
  • That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that who holds the Ironman world record? Depending on who you ask, it's Magnus Ditlev and Anne Haug, who own the fastest iron-distance time. (Photo: Ironman (Donald Miralle), Challenge Family, FinisherPix).

After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.

That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024.

And yet, despite all these amazing feats, there are no world records in full-distance racing.

Recent findings suggest that confused? It’s understandable. Pour yourself a cup of coffee and get ready to learn why Ironman (and iron-distance) world records technically don’t exist.

In the world of running, 26.2-mile marathons must adhere to rigorous certification standards set by World Athletics that include restrictions on things like point-to-point courses, elevation drop, and (recent) International measurement, but triathlon operates without such official oversight. Course configurations are notoriously inconsistent, often shifting from one season to the next, and triathletes don’t even think twice about point-to-point courses or elevation drops between start and finish.

Certainly course distances are confirmed in high-level World Triathlon races like the Olympics, but there is no course certification for long-course or for regular age-group races. Often, you’ll hear athletes remark that their GPS watch clocked an Ironman course as short or long – rarely does a race hit exactly 2.4 miles of swimming, 112 miles of cycling, and 26.2 miles of running. Those are ballpark figures that races would love to hit if they can, but permitting problems might mean the host city can only close 110 miles of roads for the bike course – this occurred at Ironman Texas in 2018, when “Ironman record times” were clocked by Melissa Hauschildt and Matt Hanson.

Beyond the logistics, an athlete’s clock is at the mercy of Mother Nature; factors like local climate, hilly terrain, or even a current-assisted swim can skew the data (as was the case in 2021, when Blummenfelt floated downcurrent to a 39:41 swim en route to a then “Ironman record” of 7:21:12 in Cozumel).

Because of that, Ironman confirmed in 2026 that they do not keep track of “official” world records for that reason, with a spokesperson telling Triathlete, “Due to variance of courses (even from year-to-year the same race could have course alterations), combined with the fact that unlike marathons, triathlon does not have official course certification for records, we use world best, course best, race best, swim/bike/run course best, etc.”.

The same holds true for Ironman 70.3 races and non-branded half-iron triathlons; no course certification, no “official” record.

Industry observers note that for what it’s worth, the Guinness World Records recognizes the “fastest time to complete an Ironman triathlon,” but not fastest iron-distance time (which we’ll explain in the next section). This may be more a function of marketing, as Ironman has established its own “partner” page on the Guinness Book of World Records website. Guinness does recognize some other triathlon records, including “fastest lumberjack triathlon,” which raises many other questions we’ll save for a different article.

Then there’s the branding gymnastics of Ironman™ versus an iron-distance race like Challenge Roth.

Sources indicate that you see, even though Challenge Roth is a 140.6-mile triathlon, it’s not an Ironman. Ironman is a distinct brand of 140.6-mile races, though many use the name to designate the distance (similar to how most Americans say “pass me a Kleenex” for tissue, or “I need a Band-Aid,” instead of requesting an adhesive bandage).

And though Challenge Roth has been around for decades, the course and race have evolved. In 2010, the Challenge Roth run course was adjusted to be more spectator-friendly, and the bike course has been altered several times for safety, most recently in 2024. In 2026, Roth expanded the pro bike drafting zone from 12 to 20 meters, creating entirely different race dynamics altogether.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, establishing a definitive “record” is difficult even for a single event, given how much can change from one year to the next. And though iron-distance “records” are often broken at Challenge Roth, they’re technically not the site of “the fastest iron-distance times in history.”.

In 2022, Kristian Blummenfelt and Kat Matthews covered the 140.6-mile distance in what would have been record-setting times of 6:44:25 and 7:31:54 – except that they did it in a unique setup involving pacers, drafting, and extra equipment as part of the Sub7/Sub8 Project. The event allowed for advanced technological and athletic optimizations, featuring specialized gear like prototype bikes and pace teams on the swim and bike to provide slipstreams for Blummenfelt and Matthews to draft off of — all things you’d never be allowed to do in a legitimate race.

This format drew considerable criticism and debate on social media, with the community questioning whether the Sub7/Sub8 times should be viewed as legitimate records. Many referenced Jan Frodeno’s 7:27:53 time for a similar iron-distance experiment known as Tri Battle Royle, which was held on a highly modified course featuring special ramps and a perfectly mapped swim line to remove tricky turns.

Because these events were so heavily optimized, no one regards these times as actual world records — just like the much-hyped 2017 Breaking2 Nike marketing event for the marathon record. Instead, they’re chalked up to fascinating experiments for fans to geek out over. (And for that, we’re thankful.).

So now that we’ve determined there is no official world record for Ironman, iron-distance triathlon, or otherwise, we can establish there are fastest-known times, with all the caveats above.

Latest Update: What the Full Moon in Gemini Means for You
