#205907. My Shimano Pedals Are Nearly 10 Years Old—This 10-Minute Service Saved Me From Spending $200 on a Fresh Set

My Shimano Pedals Are Nearly 10 Years Old—This 10-Minute Service Saved Me From Spending $200 on a Fresh Set

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that my longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance.
  • It has been revealed that I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on.
  • Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the fresh pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that my longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance. Those pedals have been effectively abused on everything from getting bashed through rock gardens to long dusty or muddy days on the gravel bike. A few years ago I got my first road bike and switched to a pair of Shimano SPD-SL pedals. Since then I’ve put that bike (and those pedals) through the wringer.

It has been revealed that I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on. This means my road pedals have seen similar abuse to my mountain bike and gravel pedals. They’re still in great shape, but they could use a little love. Even pedals only used for road riding will start to get gritty over time.

Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the fresh pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.

After I saw the rollout, it felt like a good time to bring my old generation SPD-SL pedals back to life and while I’m at it, give you a few tips on the process. Here we’ll run through how to service your SPD-SL pedals in under 10 minutes and save you a few hundred dollars in the process.

A quick note on reinstalling the pedals back on the bike: make sure you put the right pedal on the right side and the left pedal on the left side. I know, this sounds obvious. I’ve seen the wrong pedal get forced into the wrong side of the crank too many times, damaging the crank and the pedals to the point that sometimes both need to be replaced. Sometimes pedals are marked with an “L” for left and “R” for right, but you can always double-check to see which way the threads go. Left pedal threads will go up to the left and right pedal threads go up to the right. Then when it is time to reattach the pedals, put some grease on the threads of the crank arm and begin to thread them on by hand instead of starting with the wrench. If you can’t begin to thread the pedal onto the crank threads by hand, double-check the pedal is on the correct side, make sure it’s going into the crank arm straight, and make sure there is no debris in the hole of the crank arm preventing it from threading.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that our usual go-to shoe recommendation for new runners has always been the Brooks Ghost. It’s the ideal trainer to choose when you’re overwhelmed with all the offerings out there, unsure where to start or which shoe is right for you. The Ghost was a part of the quintessential runner starter pack:.

But this year was different. When we covered the Ghost 18’s release in May, our staff had already logged a few weeks of mileage in the shoe. And the verdict was... mixed.

It’s been six months since that initial testing, and during that time, the brand’s cushier model, the Brooks Glycerin 23, surpassed the Ghost in terms of popularity and positive feedback. What it all came down to was fit.

When we evaluate running shoes, we rate key attributes like weight, flexibility, and durability. Predictably, the Glycerin 23 scored a lower overall average score in weight compared to the Ghost 18 (the former is tenths of an ounce heavier than the Ghost). Other features between the shoes were relatively similar, except when it came to comfort. The Glycerin 23 received high scores, whereas the Ghost 18’s comfort was rated high by men and very low by women. The keyword here was “crammed.”.

“I had no cramming of my toes,” said Glycerin 23 tester Maura Dalek. “My feet had plenty of room to move around in and kept my feet dry and cool.”.

Juxtapose this with Ghost 18 tester and Deputy Editor Mallory Creveling’s comment: “The length was great; the width not so much...[My] forefoot area [felt] crammed the more I ran.”.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t just women testers who felt this version of the Ghost ran narrower than previous iterations. Art Director John Hamilton stated he would have felt comfier in a wider fit. Despite his discomfort, he still gave the Ghost 18 a high rating.

Recent findings suggest that like eating mushrooms or drinking a martini neat, sometimes running in a shoe is an acquired taste. While it’s not the advice I’d give to runners shopping for running shoes (“You’ll eventually love it. Really!”), it’s a pickle we sometimes allow ourselves to fall into: a model you’ve always liked and the newest one doesn’t feel the same, but you’re going to stick it out anyway.

In a recent development, so I asked testers what they thought of the Ghost 18 months later. Creveling said she gave the shoe several chances, and had maybe two pain-free runs in them.

But here’s where our testing is limited: The Ghost 18 is available in several widths, including narrow, wide, and extra wide. Our samples come in the standard width (B for women, D for men), and our testing pool includes runners of various foot shapes. Fit varies across brands, and yes, even from model to model.

Here’s one piece of gear advice I can’t emphasize enough (people in the back, do you hear me?): It’s vital to try on a shoe and go for a test run in it first before making a commitment. Another underrated piece of advice is getting your foot measured to see if you need a narrower or wider width. Your feet change over time due to aging, life events, and gravity.

One tester who had no glitch with the shoe’s fit had this to say: “High [score] overall for the latest edition of the Ghost. As an owner of previous Ghost models, this one is a worthy successor. Everything that makes the Ghost great as a daily trainer is present here—stability, durability, great on wet roads or loose gravel.” And on the fit? “Plenty of room in the toebox...Super comfortable.”.

Industry observers note that runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate was also satisfied with the Ghost 18’s comfort. “Brooks continues to nail the fit,” he said. “It’s one of the reasons I love their shoes—no matter how a model evolves, I know I’m going to get a good wrap. Even in the Ghost, which is a little more spartan for padding and luxury, it still wraps the foot well and feels good no matter how far I run.”.

He is referring to the familiar touch points we know and love about Brooks shoes: a plush heel collar that fits securely around your ankle, a flat ribbed tongue that looks like the cuffs on a cozy knit sweater.

Though the shoe doesn’t pack as powerful a punch with DNA Loft v3 foam (nitrogen-infused EVA) compared to shoes with TPEE or PEBA, it’s a reliable mile muncher, making it worthy for logging those everyday workouts when you’re building toward a race or just getting started with running.

It has been revealed that at $150, the Ghost 18 is comparable to the $145 Newly introduced Balance Ellipse. If you want a slightly heavier, cushier daily trainer that costs $175, go with the Glycerin 23. If you want a true Goldilocks shoe that’s slightly lighter with a generous amount of cushioning, go with the Ghost 18. Just consider your width options before buying!

According to recent reports, in 1977, the Vantage was the first Brooks shoe to top our charts. The running renaissance began several years prior, when Frank Shorter won the 1972 Olympic marathon in Munich. Two years later, the shoe industry would be changed forever with the introduction of ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) foam, which was lighter, softer, and had more rebound than the rubbers used in midsoles around that time. Our editors knew Brooks had a winner when we tested the Vantage.

Industry observers note that almost half a century later, the brand is still dazzling us with its innovations and earning prizes in the 2026 Runner’s World Shoe Awards. And to think the company started out more than a hundred years ago manufacturing ballet slippers and bath shoes.

It has been revealed that since the 1970s, Brooks has solely focused on upping the ante in shoe tech. The Vantage also introduced the varus wedge, which was basically a medial post used to help with instability caused by overpronation. Now the varus wedge is dated and has been replaced with Brooks’s “GuideRails” system. EVA is also being phased out with improved foams that are bouncier and even softer.

Industry observers note that our team vets hundreds of shoes a year and distributes models to more than 250 local testers for evaluation. Shoe testers of different levels, ages, arch heights, and gait patterns log at least a hundred miles before submitting feedback on a shoe’s fit, feel, and ride. Keep returning for more updates as we make our way through 2026’s hottest Brooks releases.

Sources indicate that the Glycerin 23 knocked the Ghost 18 out of Best Overall this round. While the Ghost 18 is still on this list as Best Daily Trainer, we found during testing that the Glycerin 23 is more foot shape-friendly. Testers liked the broader platform and toe room, as well as the bouncy and supportive cushioning. The shoe is my go-to for daily training—but the long run is where it shines.

I usually grab a carbon-plate shoe for my long runs, especially when I’m less confident about being out on the road for two hours at the beginning of marathon training. But the Glycerin 23’s midsole upgrade convinced me to save my carbon shoes for race day. DNA Tuned is lighter than DNA Loft, the Glycerin’s previous foam, and delivers a springier ride. My legs feel fresh when I power down hills in the shoes. The energy return doesn’t make my double-digit runs feel like a crawl.

Sources indicate that the shoe is also available as the Glycerin GTS 23, the stability counterpart. I find the Glycerin GTS 23 slightly stiffer and firmer than the neutral model, but it’s a good choice for runners who need a little more support on their long runs if they’re prone to late-onset overpronation, or if they prefer denser cushioning underfoot.

Even in the Ghost, which is a little more spartan for padding and luxury, it still wraps the foot well and feels good no matter how far I run.”.

In a recent development, the Ghost 18 is a great trainer for latest runners and those looking for a trusty workhorse to log daily mileage. However, in lieu of the Ghost 18, women and wide-foot runners may want to opt for our Best Overall, the Glycerin 23, for their daily training, instead.

Before you come at recommending an “illegal shoe” that goes well above World Athletics below-40mm guidelines, know this: marathons are hard, and the majority of athletes running them aren’t 2:30-elites—they’re runners like me and you.

Two major draws of the Hyperion Max 4: the rubber coverage on the outsole and the broader platform. Super shoes tend to skimp on rubber to save weight. Though the Hyperion Max 4 weighs more than your average racing shoe, the bouncy super foams make your runs feel effortless. And the rubber outsole provides something underrated: confidence. Running in the Hyperion Max 4, you won’t fear for your life turning sharp corners or slipping over yellow strips. After adding a full PEBA midsole to the Hyperion Elite 5, Brooks zeroed in on everything else in the next iteration of the shoe. The Hyperion Elite 6 rides more aggressively thanks to its latest geometry. The SpeedVault+ plate and RapidRoll rocker are adjusted to promote faster turnover, making those mid-race surges smooth—especially when you’re low on gas.

It has been revealed that our testers called out its accommodating fit in the midfoot area, saying it isn’t as narrow as other racing shoes they’ve tested. They appreciated the softness and comfort of the midsole as well as its propulsive bounce at marathon pace.

In a recent development, the Glycerin Flex changes the paradigm of cushioning as we know it. For one thing, its stack height is comparably low at 36mm for a cushioned trainer in a sea of high-stacked super trainers reaching beyond 40mm. The tooling on the midsole is also unlike anything we’ve seen. A diagonal midfoot Flex Zone allows you to bend the shoe in half in your hands. The pliability is meant to mimic how your foot is built, allowing your feet to flex instead of being forced to comply with stiff shoe construction.

In a recent development, the DNA Tuned cushioning is the same in the Glycerin Max and Glycerin 23. Small cells in the forefoot and large ones in the heel create a luxurious ride that absorbs shock without the foamy bulk. Lightweight and malleable, it challenges what we think when we hear cushioned trainer.

According to recent reports, “The Brooks Glycerin Flex strikes an effective balance between lightweight construction, plush cushioning, flexible midsole, comfortable fit, and outsole durability, making it well suited as an everyday trainer,” remarked tester Lindsay Vuong. “The shoe transitions easily from running to gym sessions and daily wear. I especially appreciate the padded heel, which surrounds the back of my foot like a pillow while still holding it securely in place.”.

The Adrenaline GTS turns 25, and it’s plusher and more responsive than its forebears. Just like the Ghost 17, Brooks added 1mm of cushioning to the heel and a whopping 3mm to the forefoot, making the shoe have a 10mm drop. Sources indicate that brooks’s guide rails on the lateral and medial sides of the shoe act as bumpers to align ankle and knee movement. This holistic approach to stability makes the shoe a great pick for overpronators and for neutral runners who need a little support later in their runs when their form gets sloppy This is why the Adrenaline is a long run favorite.

“I like that it felt like a normal trainer,” said Associate Service Editor Matt Rudisill, who runs with a neutral gait. “I thought these were going to be clunky and solid. Testers remarked the Vibram Megagrip outsole was a favorite feature, its 4mm lugs effectively bit into loose surfaces, handling mud and gravel well.

The Trail Adapt system—which involves a wide base, flexibility in key areas, and adaptable lugs—makes the Cascadia 20 a favorite shoe pick for runners who need more stability off-road.

The shoe felt secure and reliable on uneven terrain, though it prioritizes durability and confidence over outright speed. Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

It has been revealed that brooks has categorized its shoes to help runners choose the best pair that fits their running style and preferred experience. I’ve been a Brooks die-hard since my high school days. For the past 20 years, I’ve been keeping tabs on product updates and saying goodbye to discontinued lineups (taps for the PureProject minimalist list). Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

Industry observers note that one helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

According to recent reports, runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

At the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

Recent findings suggest that for runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Industry observers note that before the Adrenaline GTS introduced in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

According to recent reports, in 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Guide rails offer unobtrusive support for both overpronators and neutral runners.

Our lab tests show that DNA Loft remains Brooks’s softest midsole material.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

The most responsive expression of Brooks’s DNA foam debuted on the Hyperion Tempo.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

Industry observers note that we always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

Industry observers note that according to testers, the Hyperion Elite 6 feels less softer and more accommodating compared to other super shoes they’ve tested. The upcoming DNA Gold midsole adds more edge compared to the Hyperion Elite’s DNA Flash foams, with testers saying the rebound is comparable to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5.

Does Brooks have bargain-priced shoes and how do they stack up to more expensive models?

The Launch 12, included on this list, has a fit and feel almost on par with more expensive models. It’s not as responsive compared to $140 to $160 trainers due to its EVA cushioning, but it delivers a smooth ride.

Whether you’re buying for a rider in your life or upgrading your cycling computer, radar, smart trainer, or power meter on a budget, Black Friday is the best time to score substantial savings. And Garmin makes some of the best and most popular training and navigation devices for road, gravel, fitness, and mountain bike riders.

Garmin’s GPS computers, smartwatches, radar taillights, power pedals, and Tacx indoor trainers have received great reviews from Bicycling editors and top rankings in our head-to-head tests. Plus, devices can look similar at first glance, but the details matter when choosing the right tool for riding, training, and everyday fitness.

SHOP GARMIN DEALS ON AMAZON SHOP DEALS ON GARMIN.COM.

Garmin GPS head units are one of the smartest upgrades you can make to your road, gravel, mountain, or electric bike, and a much safer alternative than strapping your phone to the bars to see your route. Cycling computers also capture, process, and display data from accessories like heart rate monitors, power meters, and even electronic shifting to help you ride better, train smarter, and stay connected. And because Garmin lets you customize nearly everything—from data fields to navigation screens—you can tailor exactly what highlights up.

Sources indicate that buying Tip: Buying previous-generation cycling computers is a great way to save money. Older models usually have almost the same performance at a big discount. Cyclists often even prefer the old models if they’re lighterweight or have better battery life.

In a recent development, cycling radar is one of the most vital pieces of bicycle technology released in the last decade. On-bike radar systems mount to the rear of your bike and feature an integrated taillight. Paired with a cycling computer or smartwatch, they notify you about vehicles approaching from behind so you can move out of the way. They are a must-have item for road and gravel riders.

Buying Tip: Garmin is a pioneer in cycling radar tech and makes the most reliable, consistent systems. The Varia RTL515 is our benchmark and best-value pick, while the RearVue 820 is newer and more powerful; it’s our choice for best performance. The RCT715 is the 515 with an integrated rear-facing camera.

While dedicated cycling computers are the go-to choice for road, gravel, and data-heavy training, many riders prefer Garmin’s smartwatches because they keep everything in one place, especially when they track more than bike rides—anyone who mixes riding with running, hiking, paddling, strength training, or even walking the dog. Garmin watches have powerful GPS, workout metrics, and daily health data in a streamlined device that’s always with you (and they even tell time).

Buying Tip: Mountain bikers often appreciate the simplicity and safety of recording their rides from the wrist rather than risking a pricey head unit in a crash. Triathletes, duathletes, and cyclocross racers love the seamless transitions a watch allows. There’s no need to swap devices or merge files after an event.

Most riders know Garmin from its computers, smartwatches, and cycling radar. But Garmin also owns the indoor trainer brand Tacx. Its smart trainers and indoor bikes are highly regarded for their excellent performance, integration, and useful features. One cool feature we love—especially if you live somewhere prone to winter power outages—is that the Neo 2T generates its own resistance electromagnetically. That means you don’t have to scrap your workout plans just because the lights go out.

Recent findings suggest that buying Tip: Smart trainers are great for riding in virtual worlds like Zwift. For a deep dive into more great indoor trainers and buying info, check out my story “Ready to Ride Indoors? Here’s How to Pick the Best Trainer.”.

Garmin Tacx Neo 2T with Zwift Cog and Click.

Garmin Tacx Flux2 Smart Trainer.

Want to step up your training for next season? The best way to measure cycling gains is by training with power—and for that, you need a power meter. Power pedals, like Garmin’s Rally series, are easier to install than crank-based power meter options. Plus, you can swap power pedals easily between bikes. This not only saves cost, but it also gives you consistent data from bike to bike.

Buying Tip: Garmin offers a handy option to buy its power meter in a package including two pedal styles (road and mountain bike/gravel) with swappable spindles. This way you can measure power across riding disciplines.

Recent findings suggest that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Fresh England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Tech Report: Josh Kerr Notes You Probably Don’t Need Water for Runs Under 12 Miles. The Internet Had Thoughts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant.
  • So when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from.
  • "I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr said, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant. The two bottles bounced loosely against my chest, with water leaking down my shirt throughout the run. It was not a flattering look. Every step came with its own sloshing soundtrack. I spent so much time adjusting the thing (despite an across-the-chest strap) that I barely enjoyed my run.

So when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from. During a Reddit AMA hosted by BBC Sport, the Scottish middle-distance star, who casually broke the mile world record in July with a 3:42.66 finish, shared his thoughts on the growing popularity of running vests.

"I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr said, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.

For context, we're talking about a world-record holder, Olympic medalist, and world champion in the 1500 meters. He knows a thing or two about logging miles. And while 12 miles might look quite different on his watch than mine, I don't think his suggestion was particularly outrageous.

And because everything is contested on the internet, plenty of people disagree.

Sources indicate that runner @natalie.the.capn shared Kerr's comments on Threads and explained that she wears a hydration belt on every outing so she has somewhere to keep her phone, particularly in case of an emergency. "Funny how men rarely think of that," she wrote.

I do understand her concern. I'm a guy, so I'm definitely not going to pretend I have the same safety considerations that women often face while exercising alone. I also bring my phone everywhere, usually carrying it in my hand because iPhones only get bigger and the pockets on most of my running shorts haven't kept up.

She also pointed out that some of her routes take her six miles or more between places where she can get water, which is an entirely different experience from mine.

I live in Latest York City, where Central Park has plenty of water fountains (that work ... most of the time) and there's usually a deli within walking distance to snag a Gatorade. I can see why Kerr's approach makes sense here, especially for shorter runs. I've also tried handheld bottles and waist straps, and neither has been particularly enjoyable. Between the bouncing, adjusting, and occasional hand cramps, I'd love to carry as little as possible in my hands.

In a recent development, that changes a lot during marathon training, something I've put myself through four times now, when I'm out for considerably longer and need water to wash down those pasty gels. Aside from the hydration aspect, stopping to buy something, pausing my watch, and interrupting my stride halfway through a long run is a vibe killer.

In a recent development, and I'm certainly not arguing against being prepared. I learned the hard way that sunscreen deserved a permanent spot in my prerun routine after years of neglecting it ended with some casual skin cancer surgery.

Sources indicate that the Threads debate, naturally, has brought out some pretty different opinions. One commenter, siding with Kerr, wrote, "Yeah im gonna listen to the guy who runs for a living but thanks." Others pointed out that beginners, slower runners, and people training in hot weather could have very different hydration needs.

Sources indicate that they're definitely right about that. Twelve miles is a long way for plenty of runners, no matter what their experience level, and access to water, weather, pace, and individual needs all change the equation. Kerr even acknowledged that people have different reasons for carrying gear, something that seems to have gotten a little lost as his comments made their way around social media.

I still think he has a fair point about how much equipment we sometimes convince ourselves we need on a run. That said, if your vest makes your runs more comfortable or gives you peace of mind, by all means wear it. For me, I'll be keeping my phone close and bringing an appropriate amount of water when I need it.

As for my hydration vest, it's been collecting dust ever since that first outing, and I haven't missed it one bit.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than 24 hours after his third-place finish at WTCS Abu Dhabi, Hayden Wilde (NZL) showed few outward signs of fatigue as he hit the front of the race in T1, rode among the leaders, and ran his way to victory ahead of training partner Kyle Smith (NZL).

In a recent development, georgia Taylor-Brown stated before the race that she wanted to “beat Julie,” and her wish came true. A small breakaway in the swim put Derron (SUI) on the back foot from the start, while Taylor-Brown had to overcome cramps on the bike and a charging Nicole Van Der Kaay (NZL) on the run to earn a narrow, yet vital victory.

It was a mixed cast of T100 veterans and rookies on the men’s start line, with several notable names absent after the men’s Saudi Arabia T100 race was moved to Dubai on short notice.

Big news leading into the race was that RaceRanger devices would not be used on the bike due to customs delays in getting the equipment into Dubai, leaving officials to enforce the 20-meter draft zone without the light sensor system.

Industry observers note that A large group emerged from the tepid water to start the bike. After a subpar swim left Wilde chasing in Abu Dhabi the day before, he not only swam with the front group but sprinted through transition, smiling and chatting as he rounded Rico Bogen (GER), showing little sign of the previous day’s effort.

He took his time putting on full-length aero socks as Menno Koolhaas (NED) went straight to the front to lead the men onto the scorching tarmac for 80km of time trialing on the flat course.

The group of 17 after the swim promptly whittled down to 10 as average speeds approached 30 mph in the opening stages.

As Bogen, Wilde, and Smith continued to push the pace, the group promptly dropped to just six. The standout name among the group was Mika Noodt (GER), back racing for the first time since his collision with an ambulance at Ironman 70.3 Swansea in July and already taking turns at the front.

Noodt had been one of the sport’s biggest up-and-coming stars before the accident and was to be Wilde’s strongest challenger on the T100 circuit this year. He has openly shared the mental struggles and trauma that followed the crash, but it seemed he was back to full strength on course as the German powered toward the run.

Recent findings suggest that off the bike, a quick transition saw Wilde round Bogen for the lead, and he looked set to run away without a challenge. Smith, however, quickly moved alongside him and stayed there for the opening laps until Wilde turned up the heat.

According to recent reports, from there, there was no stopping him as he put last year’s lap-counting drama in Dubai behind him to head into the Qatar final with a perfect score from his three counting results. Smith held on for his best T100 result of the year, ahead of an emotional Noodt, who marked his return with an immediate trip to the podium.

One of the most remarkable revelations came afterward, when Wilde shared that he believed he had raced much of the day with a broken toe. He injured it during the Aussie exit on the swim and, thinking it might be dislocated, tried to pop it back into place during the bike. Despite the swelling afterward, he stated it had not troubled him too much on the run.

A front group of four broke away early on the swim as Taylor-Brown and Kate Waugh’s (GBR) blueprint to put Derron under pressure from the start worked perfectly. Waugh led through the Aussie exit before Sara Pérez Sala (ESP) led the group into T1.

Derron found herself almost a minute down, but alongside strong riders Caroline Pohle (GER) and Van der Kaay, she remained well within contention. The substantial question was whether her efforts in Kona would affect her race or whether the heat preparation would prove beneficial in the sweltering conditions.

Industry observers note that on the bike, it appeared to be the former as Pohle and Van der Kaay left her behind and worked their way to the front. They eventually helped put more time into Derron, who was over two minutes back and still losing ground on the third lap.

It was not an unfamiliar position for Derron, who had overcome a deficit at the previous women’s race in Vancouver to take down Taylor-Brown and Waugh.

In a recent development, however, it soon became clear that only Taylor-Brown would remain in the fight for the win, with Waugh’s race unraveling in the heat. She later shared on social media that she had started the race sick but still managed to get across the line in ninth, her first T100 finish off the podium.

Sources indicate that everything was going according to plan for Taylor-Brown until she began suffering from adductor cramps late on the bike. She lost positions as she tried to soft-pedal them out, but thankfully for her, they subsided enough for her to start the run just 36 seconds behind Pohle, with Van der Kaay and Pérez Sala also ahead.

Taylor-Brown’s cramps were well in her rearview as she quickly made up the gap and began building a lead. By the third lap, it looked as though that advantage might continue to grow all the way to the finish.

Industry observers note that however, Van der Kaay was putting together the best T100 performance of her career and began closing again heading into the final lap. Derron had moved into third but was not making any significant inroads into either athlete ahead.

It has been revealed that van der Kaay put in one final surge to try to catch Taylor-Brown but came up just 10 seconds short. The victory now sends Taylor-Brown into the Grand Final six points clear of Derron and in pole position to become world champion.

Van der Kaay’s excellent performance, which included the second-fastest bike and third-fastest run, moves her into third in the standings heading into the final.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking.
  • I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking. They can also make simple jobs harder than they need to be. Adjusting your position can mean cutting a steerer tube. Replacing a broken handlebar can mean buying a whole fresh cockpit. And routing brake hoses through everything can turn a small change into a long afternoon.

I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews. It’s proprietary, and integrated systems come with real compromises. But after swapping the drops on the Endurace CF SLX 9 I have in for review, I want to give Canyon credit for a thoughtful design choice.

Sources indicate that the main section of the PACE cockpit is called the T-Bar. Canyon’s system lets you adjust cockpit height by up to 20 mm in 5mm increments, without cutting the steerer. The cockpit is also made up of three pieces, with the drop sections bolted to the T-Bar. That offers a couple of advantages.

First, it makes the bar width adjustable. The T-Bar has three width positions, 25 mm apart, for a total range of 50 mm. The actual widths depend on the drop shape. See the table below.

In a recent development, the bolt-on drops also let Canyon offer five shapes with different dimensions. If the drops that come on your new Canyon don’t suit you, you can swap them for another option.

In a recent development, my Endurace review bike came with the Compact drops. They have a 108mm drop, width settings from 390 to 440 mm, and 8 degrees of flare. I prefer a narrower bar with a deeper drop and more flare, so I switched to Canyon’s Control drops. They have a 120mm drop, adjust from 370 to 420 mm, and feature 17 degrees of flare.

*U.S. prices at the time of writing. Bar tape and fixing screws are included.

In a recent development, here’s what I needed to do to make the swap: unwrap the bar, loosen and slide off the controls, remove the old drops, install the latest ones, then tighten everything and rewrap the bar. Canyon includes fresh bar tape with the replacement drops.

Canyon also includes a clever cardboard tool that helps you evenly align your controls. I loved it!

It has been revealed that with most one-piece integrated cockpits, switching to a different bar shape or replacing a broken drop means replacing the whole assembly. Depending on the bike’s routing, that may also mean disconnecting or replacing brake hoses and bleeding the brakes.

Sources indicate that on the PACE, the brake hoses run behind the drop sections rather than through them, so I didn’t have to disconnect or cut them. That meant no brake bleed, no risk of ending up with a hose that’s too short, and no replacing the entire cockpit.

That also matters if you crash and break a drop. With a one-piece handlebar and stem, a broken bar can mean replacing the whole assembly. With PACE, you can replace the damaged section.*.

In a recent development, *If you break a drop, check the PACE T-Bar, or stem, for damage, too. Replace it if necessary.

In a recent development, the system can also make bike travel less nerve-racking. If your bar tape is set up so the controls can slide on and off without rewrapping, you can unbolt the drops and let them hang out of the way. The bike packs a little narrower, and the handlebar ends are less exposed to side impacts. I’ve had bars damaged in transit more times than I can count, so I appreciate this feature.

PACE is still proprietary, and those concerns don’t disappear because one part of the system is clever. But integrated cockpits often force riders to accept limited adjustability, few shape options, and costly replacements. Canyon has found a useful way to make its handlebar easier to fit, repair, and travel with. For that, it deserves some credit.

According to recent reports, A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success.
  • In a recent development, learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World.
  • Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success. Go out too hard and you may struggle to hold on. Run too conservatively and you might miss your goal finish.

In a recent development, learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World. One workout he recommends for building this skill is a fartlek he learned from fellow run coach Brad Hudson, his coauthor on the book, Run Faster from the 5K to the Marathon: How to Be Your Own Best Coach.

Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them. The goal? Building both aerobic fitness and a greater sense of pace control.

This workout helps improve your ability to settle into the right effort earlier, as well as enhance your capacity to hold those paces for longer—a perfect session for both optimizing your weekly speed run and helping you run your fastest race.

After an easy running warmup, you’ll run five faster segments, separated by an easy jog of the same duration.

The base workout uses three target paces: 5K pace for the one-minute segments, 10K pace for the two-minute segments, and half-marathon pace for the three-minute segment. If you don’t know your race paces, you can also go off of rate of perceived exertion (RPE), with 10 equaling all-out effort. You should still be able to have a conversation around 4 RPE.

It has been revealed that fitzgerald states the workout should feel “fun hard,” meaning the faster running should feel challenging, but you shouldn’t finish the workout feeling like you just went all out in a race. Each surge is relatively short, so focus on hitting your intended effort rather than pushing as hard as you can.

More experienced, higher-volume runners can extend the pyramid to 1-2-3-2-1-2-3-2-1, again jogging for the same duration after each faster segment. This version includes 17 minutes of faster running and 17 minutes of recovery jogging, compared to just nine minutes of each in the original version.

In Fitzgerald’s experience, many runners tend to think of their effort in two broad categories: slow and fast, but this workout challenges that by demanding more care in differentiating between faster paces.

In a recent development, the one-minute 5K pace efforts should be faster than the two-minute 10K pace efforts, which should be faster than the three-minute half-marathon effort, explains Fitzgerald. The differences between these three paces are small—often just a few seconds per mile—so learning to recognize what each one feels like can help you become a more efficient and more confident runner.

According to recent reports, before each segment, think about the effort you’re trying to find. For the first one-minute interval, Fitzgerald suggests literally imagining that you’re starting a 5K race. You wouldn’t want to sprint the opening minute of that race and flame out, so resist that urge here, too.

Try to settle into the right pace by feel, then use your watch to check and adjust. Over time, you’ll grow more attuned to the connection between how you feel and how fast you’re moving. “Your watch can’t [run the workout] for you,” Fitzgerald states. “It can tell you how fast you’re going. It can’t tell you how fast you should go.”.

Sources indicate that learning to run by feel translates to race day, when you want to hit your goal pace. Your body’s response to the conditions and the effort helps you decide how to proceed through each mile, slowing down or speeding up.

It has been revealed that this workout doesn’t ask you to spend a long time at any single pace. Instead, it gives you short exposures to several intensities within one session.

Hudson, who’s coached multiple Olympians and world-class athletes, tells Runner’s World that moving through a range of paces during a single workout helps with not only pace control, but also running economy or the energy required to run at a given speed.

Additionally, Hudson explains the continuous nature of the fartlek session gives it an aerobic emphasis because you never actually stop running throughout the entirety of the workout. “The faster portions [of the workout] increase oxygen demand, but as you go longer in a workout, the more it becomes aerobic, no matter what,” he states. “If you’re keeping the running continuous, the aerobic energy systems just keep going up and up and up.”.

Recent findings suggest that fitzgerald agrees, although he also notes athletes get some anaerobic stress during the shorter, faster efforts. Think of it as a way to work on several aspects of your fitness at once, rather than a session designed to train just one. Plus, switching between paces can make the workout more mentally engaging than returning to the same effort over and over again.

Sources indicate that the first time you try the workout, you might overshoot a target pace or find it difficult to feel the difference between efforts. That’s okay. Fitzgerald says trial and error is an important part of developing the skill.

When you repeat the session, look for signs that your pacing is becoming more controlled: You start each segment closer to your intended effort, settle into a steadier rhythm, and maintain a clear difference between your 5K, 10K, and half marathon paces. You may also find it easier to keep your recovery jogs consistent.

According to recent reports, the point is, you don’t need to nail every second of this workout. Learn from your mistakes, adjust when necessary, and remember Fitzgerald’s advice: “Progress over perfection.”.

It has been revealed that it may be tempting to think of the easy jogs simply as passing time between hard segments. But both coaches emphasize the value of continuous running and implore runners not to lose focus during the recovery intervals.

Fitzgerald notes teaching your body to recover from a faster effort while still moving presents a unique challenge. Your muscles must learn how to continue producing the energy needed to keep you running efficiently while your body works to recover from the harder interval at the same time. This adaptation translates directly to race day when you have to settle back into race pace after surging to pass another runner or gliding a little too fast down a hill.

The key is paying attention to how your recovery intervals feel. If you have to slow them down more and more to prepare for the next segment, Fitzgerald claims that may be a sign you’re pushing the faster portions too hard.

The beauty of this workout is if you realize you’ve gone out too promptly, you can easily adjust so you can still complete the workout. If you overcooked one of your speedier segments, Fitzgerald suggests tacking on another minute or so to the easy jog until you breathe easier and lower your heart rate—then adjust your effort level on the next interval.

Because the workout touches several intensity levels, Fitzgerald recommends it during base training or in the off-season. It can help runners maintain well-rounded fitness before they begin building toward a more specific goal.

It can also work as the de facto speed workout during a lighter training week or serve as a secondary quality workout during half-marathon or marathon training. In this case, the session offers a chance to maintain some faster running while the biggest emphasis remains on your long runs and race-specific efforts.

Hudson uses the workout as a key tool in returning to training post-marathon. After a week off, he generally has his athletes begin with easy running. Then, he adds this workout as a way to reintroduce different intensity levels and prepare his athletes for more demanding work ahead.

Whenever you use it, keep its purpose in mind: It’s designed to help you practice changing gears and build general fitness, and using it to support key workouts specifically tailored to your next race makes it even more effective.

Time Off Feet Will Change How You Think About Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress.
  • Now, as a Latest York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training aims.
  • According to recent reports, while time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress. Absolutely not, was his answer. “It’s not as if he would have assigned me a specific time off feet metric,” Inman states, “but my feet needed to rest, and being a waitress was too much time on feet for someone racing the way I did.”.

Now, as a Latest York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training aims. For example, a nurse who is “always on her feet,” can’t have runs that overload her so much that she couldn’t keep training or working after a race, Inman indicates.

According to recent reports, while time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way. “We do have an old saying, ‘Never stand when you can sit and never sit when you can lie down,’” notes Will Baldwin, USATF and VDOT-certified running coach. Like any generalization, though, that rule isn’t very helpful.

Additionally, despite the many ways runners dig into their metrics and researchers look at small running form and running shoe discrepancies, there is little hard science regarding how much time off your feet you need and how you should best spend that time.

“Instead, you want to use comfort as your paradigm or framework on whether your recovery method is working for you,” states Jim Jastifer, MD, a fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon specializing in foot and ankle reconstruction with OSMC Orthopedic and Sports Medicine Center in Indiana.

🏃🏻‍♀️The Runner’s World Guide to Recovery is your home for a smarter—from managing soreness and fatigue to easing back into running after a race, offseason, or injury.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, “be comfortable” and “do what makes you happy” may be the best metrics for recovery, according to Jastifer. That’s because it’s not just your feet that need a break—so does your brain.

Are joy and time off feet really related? Turns out, they are. Kara Goucher, distance runner extraordinaire and cohost with Des Linden of the running podcast Nobody Asked Us, has her own way of making sure she gives herself enough time off feet.

“I love playing Sudoku!” Goucher remarked on the pod, and she considers her game playing part of her rest and recovery. “It’s time off feet that really does calm my mind and it’s so much better for my brain and mental health than doom scrolling on my phone! It's time to reset my body and my mind.”.

In fact, according to the experts, your goal around recovery and time off feet should be to become self-aware of what your body needs, what your feet need (which may be different than what your larger muscles and soft tissues need), and what your brain needs.

Sources indicate that your feet may actually be the best way to determine how to spend your recovery time; your wearable likely doesn’t correlate its opinion of your recovery to the stress that your feet feel, Jastifer notes. “If your Garmin says you’re ready to run, but your feet hurt, you should listen to your feet,” he adds.

According to recent reports, “Someone who is running 70/80/100 miles a week isn’t going to recover more by going for a walk,” says Baldwin. This is precisely why Inman’s coach didn’t want her, a professional runner at the time, to add waitressing on top of her training schedule.

“Instead, I try to get my athletes to do low-level movement, such as time on the bike.” For his own time off feet, Baldwin saves his favorite demonstrates to watch during these sessions so he has less mental taxation.

“Swelling and pain are really the only two reasons you absolutely need to stay off your feet,” indicates Baldwin. However, you’ll need to be aware of the difference between swelling due to injury and swelling that occurs simply because fluid has gone to your feet because of extensive motion.

“Keeping your feet in motion can actually help swelling,” claims Jastifer. Walking can stimulate the movement of blood and lymph (a fluid that carries nutrients to your blood and tissues), which can help recovery, but only if your feet aren’t fighting injury. Signs of injury include pain and discoloration.

Recent findings suggest that of course, you don’t always have to walk—or do anything with impact—to move your feet. Making circles, rolling a ball under them, or stretching them can reduce the swelling. Again, though, if you feel pain, stop and go to a doctor before you run again.

Percell Dugger, Runna run coach, suggests that you always consider rest and recovery within the context of your training blueprint, and, if your feet hurt, balance that notable metric against the intensity and effort of a planned workout, even if it’s active recovery.

It has been revealed that “In practice and by observation everyone recovers differently,” Inman says. “So, you want to be responsive to whether your feet are telling you they need to rest. If so, maybe get in a pool or get on a bike.”.

Even though there is no clear time or method for recovery, the most important thing to do between runs is sleep and eat, advises Kristine Sweezey, PT, DPT, CSCS, a physical therapist in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and Charlotte, North Carolina.

According to recent reports, jastifer agrees, adding that rest, cross-training, and time off feet are not at all the same as sleeping. “They serve different functions,” he adds. Without sleep and proper nutrition, athletes cannot actually begin to recover. Moreover, any tricks or tools you use outside of sleep and proper fueling won’t add anything to the recovery equation without a commitment to the basics.

It has been revealed that between sleep, time on feet, and time off feet, the experts recommend that you add foot strengthening to your routine. Because improving the abilities of your intrinsic foot muscles will help your feet cope with long and hard miles on the road. So, what are your intrinsic foot muscles? The small muscles that connect within your foot, but not to areas outside of it, such as your Achilles. The muscles in your toes and arch are intrinsic.

“By analogy, we have all the same muscles in our feet that we have in our hands, and while they aren’t significant from a force standpoint, they help regulate the force proprioception in ankle stability and are part of a neuromuscular feedback loop so you don’t have to think about how your feet land which will provide you with stability,” Jastifer states. “If you have foot pain, it might be from these muscles.”.

In a recent development, sweezey agrees and claims you should do all the toe scrunches and toe lifts that you can. “I keep a lacrosse ball under my desk to roll around with my feet,” she says. “It helps decrease the soreness and flushes things out.”.

In a recent development, finally, when you are ready to get back on the road with your revived feet—whether it’s been a day or a week—make sure you don’t pair two long runs or speed workouts back-to-back, indicates Dugger. “Progressive loading is better than high spikes and a dive.” If you and your feet (and your brain) need a break, don’t push too much on your next run.

Donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.

Latest Update: I Rode My Road Bike Where the Pavement Ends to Find Out How Much Gravel It Could Handle

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Just as the seasons change, so do riders’ preferences of which types of riding are preferred.
  • Many of us have tried to take our road bikes on gravel, and there are steps you can take to get the most out of that underbiked gravel ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Just as the seasons change, so do riders’ preferences of which types of riding are preferred. For some, the season for taking the road bike on the local roads starts to fade as temperatures get colder and the gravel trail that parallels the road gets more appealing every degree cooler. It’s time to turn the road bike onto that gravel path.

Many of us have tried to take our road bikes on gravel, and there are steps you can take to get the most out of that underbiked gravel ride. After a recent lunch ride, the question was asked, “how much gravel can you take a road bike on?” Since gravel means different things to different people the easy answer is, it depends, but I wanted to stress test my road bike to find out.

I remember an old-school bike technician I used to work with told me, “you can ride any bike on anything if you are light on the bike and find the right line.” While that may be true, I wanted to find out how I could most comfortably take my road bike on everything that is off-road.

After taking my road bike where it was not designed to go, I learned some limitations as well as some simple part swaps to get the most versatility out of a road bike. Below I’ll touch on those limitations that I found and give you the most impactful changes you can make to your road bike before taking it on gravel. As Doc says to Marty McFly in Back to the Future, “Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.”.

It has been revealed that the bike I decided to do the testing on is my Trek Madone, and I’ve had 700x28mm Pirelli P Zero Race tires pretty much since I’ve built up the bike. Those are by far my favorite road tires for all-around road riding—they’re fast, grip well through turns, and are surprisingly durable for performing so well.

It has been revealed that even though I love those Pirellis for road riding most of the year, I knew I would want to have extra rubber when I’m chattering along through some of the chunkier gravel I’d be testing on. I decided to swap out my tires for a set of the Continental Grand Prix 5000 in 700x32 mm. The maximum tire width on the Gen 8 Trek Madone is 32mm, but these Continental tires only measure just over 30mm because of the internal rim width on the stock Bontrager wheels. I could probably bump up the width a bit more, but I decided to keep the 32mm just in case I knock the wheels out of true during the stress testing.

According to recent reports, going wider with your tires adds an extra bit of compliance and more contact patch—both will help your ride quality when you take your road bike out on gravel. Part of the trick with going wider and bumping down your tire pressure is to make sure your tires are set up as tubeless. Setting your tires up tubeless allows you to run a lower tire pressure without the risk of pinch flats.

When you take your road bike on gravel, upcoming bar tape can help by decreasing a little bit of the vibration. As you ride, most bar tapes compress a bit from the constant pressure of your hands. Some tapes may even start to unravel in sections where you keep your hands a lot—we used to see this a lot when customers couldn’t comfortably reach the hoods. There would be visible wear marks where the rider was keeping their hands on the bars. So replacing your tape at least once a season is a good idea to keep comfort up.

Out of all the bar tape that I’ve tried my favorite for taking a road bike on gravel is the Lizard Skin 3.2 mm Bar Tape. The slightly thicker tape reduces a bit of the chatter in your hands and it’s tacky enough that your hands stay stuck to the bars when you need them to be. This is true on wider tire gravel bikes as well, but it’s especially noticeable when you don’t have the same vibration dampening from a wider tire.

It has been revealed that flat tires happen on any bike, but they can be even more common rolling down a chunky gravel road on your road bike. Correct tire choice, tubeless setups, and riding a bit more cautiously than normal will all help prevent a ride-ending flat tire.

It has been revealed that if you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multitool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

If you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multi tool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

Sources indicate that keep in mind it’s still possible to get flat tires with tubeless tires. A few years ago I took my road bike out on a local gravel ride and I bumped my tire pressure down to have a little more comfort and traction on my skinny road tires. I was rolling through some gravel and I hit a rock with my rear wheel hard enough for the tire to get pinched against the rim and put a good slice in my tire. Luckily I brought a tire boot (I used a dollar bill) and an extra tube so I was able to pedal back to the shop. In a pinch I’ve used things like candy wrappers or leaves as a very temporary tire boot. They don’t take up much room in your pack, so if you bring one in your pack there is no need to MacGyver anything on the side of the trail.

In a recent development, if you only have a road bike and want to occasionally ride gravel I would strongly consider getting a second wheelset to ride gravel. If you have one wheel set for gravel and one for pavement you can easily swap wheel sets when you want to ride one discipline versus the other. Set up the wheels with a cassette with the same gear range, same size rotors, and the widest tires your frame and fork can fit—suddenly you have two bikes in one.

As I was taking my road bike on exceedingly questionable terrain I thought, what would most people actually be okay with riding this bike on? As I rolled my Madone into some singletrack it was promptly apparent most people wouldn’t be stoked to follow behind me. Insufficient tire clearance, room for tread, and lack of suspension might be the first reasons you’d think of why a road bike isn’t going to perform well on singletrack (and you’re absolutely right). The geometry of the Madone didn’t give the handling needed to reasonably navigate through the tight trails in the woods.

It has been revealed that the next category is where we start to delve into true gravel: doubletrack, jeep roads, and limited maintenance gravel. This is where I started to see the road bike actually perform reasonably well. The extra tire width combined with bumping down the tire pressure allowed the bike to feel reasonably compliant rolling through the varying surfaces. However, I really felt the times I caught a small rock that was hiding underneath the leaves.

Riding local gravel roads and canal trails may have been bumpy, but it was most certainly doable. I noticed I was bumping around a lot, and I felt like I was putting in more effort to match my typical effort on the same segments I usually ride with a gravel bike. Especially when I started to ride through gravel after a bit of rain or sections that were covered in wet leaves I wished for a wider tire with more tread. I had to keep some of the descents a little more tame compared to normal, but on my local gravel climbs I was rolling up faster and more efficiently than normal. That is, until my rear tire would lose traction and I would burn all my matches trying to keep the bike both upright and going up.

According to recent reports, even with that being the case, so many modern road bikes now offer tire clearance to get a cyclocross tire set up. If I were committing to my road bike as a gravel-to-road crossover bike for the winter I would set it up with some fast-rolling tubeless cyclocross tires, put on upcoming bar tape, put an extra tube in my flat pack, and let it ride.

The Triathlete editorial team has been around long enough that we’ve collectively written dozens of holiday gift guides — from stocking stuffers to price point round-ups to personality-based ideas, always solid ideas but usually pretty generic.

Industry observers note that but this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

And we are happy to share our IRL gift ideas with you for your own gifting or wish list creation. Below, you’ll find out a little bit more about some of our favorite contributors, what we gifted them, and why we think they’ll enjoy it.

According to recent reports, about the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

In a recent development, what we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

According to recent reports, about the contributor: Sierra is a skilled writer who has lent her talents to highlight the need for more athlete-friendly pregnancy and postpartum deferral policies and to advocate for clearer policies around breastfeeding and pumping during races. She’s a mom to an active toddler.

In a recent development, what we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

—Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

In a recent development, about the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. From her home in Boulder, Colorado, she interviews experts, talks to today’s top pro athletes, and writes to make changes and news of the sport understandable to all athletes.

What we gifted (and why): Winters in Colorado are long and cold, making training challenging. As a tri nerd, I think Emma-Kate will enjoy keeping up with her training indoors using the latest swim tech. While I don’t think ZWIM will keep her from the gym (I’m not sure anything could), I do think it will complement her training nicely to make the winter not feel so long.

About the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

Industry observers note that what we gifted (and why): Naturally, when I read Mike Reilly’s book, Finding Your Finish Line, I thought of Tim. Reilly, also known as the “Voice of Ironman,” confirmed over 350,000 athletes across the finish line during his career as a race announcer before retiring in 2022. He, too, has seen it all, and some of his best tales are in this book. If I could get Tim and Mike in the same room to swap stories, it would probably be the best day of my triathlon career.

Recent findings suggest that reilly’s book, co-written with Triathlete contributor Sarah Wassner Flynn, is a masterful piece of storytelling. It’s inspirational, aspirational, and will leave you feeling proud to be a triathlete.

According to recent reports, about the contributor: Susan is a board-certified sports dietitian, accomplished Ironman athlete and Kona qualifier, and runs her own business helping endurance athletes dial in their health and performance goals through their nutrition. She is our go-to writer whenever we need a sports nutrition concept or topic broken down in a way that triathletes can apply to their own training and racing.

It has been revealed that what we gifted (and why): I’ve been a long-time fan of Skratch Labs for its simple ingredients and clean flavors. When we saw Skratch now offers a make-it-yourself gel-making kit using its super high-carb sports drink mix, we thought the nutrition expert who literally wrote our guide on high-carb fueling might enjoy easily customizing her nutrition intake. More than the fueling customization, the kit also provides a less gooey gel texture and planet-friendly reusable soft flasks. I’m eager to hear how it works for her!

—Bethany Mavis, contributing editor.

About the contributor: When college student Saqib came on board as an intern in our Endurance department, the first question I had for this gangly cross-country runner was, “Have you done a triathlon?” The answer was no, and I am making it my life’s mission to change that.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): Did Saqib ask for resources on triathlon? He did not. In fact, he thinks of himself as a land animal and has no interest in swimming, which is why I’m gifting him this book from Triathlete contributor Alison Freeman – just to plant the seed. Isn’t that what holiday gifts are for, anyway? Subtle hints wrapped in shiny paper? I think of my brother-in-law, who always gifts his wife exercise equipment even though she is a couch potato; or my mother, who has given me countless hairstyling tools to tame my wild mane into something she deems more respectable.

But this book will actually serve its purpose, because Freeman has a real talent for making a big, scary goal like a first triathlon approachable and achievable. Her book is a start-to-finish roadmap that eliminates guesswork and leaves the reader feeling like they can not only do a triathlon, but also have fun along the way.

About the contributor: Jon Dorn is a former editor, longtime triathlete, and lifetime gear geek. He’s qualified for six age-group world championships, and loves to bust his butt training for long-course tri. If I hear about a cutting-edge piece of gear, an unconventional training method, or something that’s just plain weird, I call Jon. That said, he’s not afraid to call a spade a spade and let me know if something is just pricey junk; he’s no fanboy.

In a recent development, what we gifted (and why): I had heard about red light therapy in the context of the general health/beauty space for a few years, but it wasn’t until I was wandering the expo in Kona at this year’s Ironman World Championship that I encountered a red light therapy device that not only targeted triathletes but is also portable. Sadly, the one I checked out on the Significant Island was bonkers expensive and didn’t make sense for a gift, so I shopped around for something similar that wouldn’t break the bank. I landed on the reasonably priced Valo Spark that had decent reviews.

In a recent development, on one hand, I’m not 100% sold on the efficacy of red light therapy — and the science is still out on how it works with sports-related aches and pains — but I know Jon trains super hard (his next race is Boulder 70.3 in June), I know he has his share of aches and pains, I know he loves to travel, and I know he likes trying new things. Whether he loves it or uses it as a portable night light, I can’t wait to find out what he thinks!

The SP Force AXS is our flagship triathlon bike, with a full carbon fiber frame and bars, built with SRAM Force electronic shifting and Zipp 404 Firecrest Carbon wheels. If you want the best performance along with the best value in triathlon, now’s your chance. Our limited BFCM sale is live now.

About the contributor: Arguably one of the most accomplished triathletes in Triathlete’s contributor lineup, with hundreds of triathlons and well over a dozen Ironmans under her belt, Jordan knows the sport from every perspective. She’s also one of the industry’s best-known and loved figures, representing professional athletes and helping brands grow their businesses.

Recent findings suggest that few people know the triathlon world better than Jordan, past or present. (She’s our first pick for a triathlon trivia team.) With her finger on the pulse, she gives pros and age-groupers a voice and digs into the stories shaping the sport.

What we gifted (and why): Jordan might spend more time in the saddle than any of us editors, and she knows her gear as well as anyone, especially what the pros are presently using. While she’s right now on the road to recovery from a meniscus tear, we wanted to send her something custom and pro-level to test whether the 3D investment matches the marketing as she rebuilds her fitness on the bike.

But saddles are tricky to gift. Finding this fully adjustable, 3D-printed option gave us the versatility we were looking for: a fit she could fine-tune herself, without being limited to the stock setup straight out of the box.

—Travis Mundell, social media manager.

About the contributor: Zach Nehr is another one of our key tech/gear editors, especially when it comes to indoor training. Blessed (or cursed) by living in the not-winter-compatible state of Wisconsin, Zach is a die-hard Zwifty and has used probably just about every indoor trainer or virtual training platform that exists (or has existed). As much as Zach rides inside, I trust that if he states something is great, it’s great; if it’s not, it’s probably in the dumpster. Because you don’t ride inside as much as he does with junk.

Recent findings suggest that what we gifted (and why): The Profile Design Zwift Ride Supersonic Aerobar was a medium-quiet release during this year’s Hawaii Ironman World Championship week – mostly because you don’t think much about riding in the pain cave when you’re in a tropical paradise prepping for the biggest race of your season. As incongruous as the setting was for an indoor release, I was excited to see that Profile was taking its triathletes seriously by announcing the first-ever triathlon-specific Zwift-integrated aerobar for indoor training.

In a recent development, I wanted to gift this to Zach because if you dedicate enough time to training indoors, you should really dedicate your indoor training setup as well, not just make do. Being able to control your avatar from a dedicated set of Zwift Ride–compatible aerobars is the pinnacle of tri gear, as it completes the perfect pain cave: the kind that could prep you for next year’s Ironman World Championship, anyway.

About the contributor: When it comes to explaining sports psychology and neuroscience studies to triathletes, there’s no one better than Daya. As a neuroscientist, certified mental performance consultant, and yogi, Daya helps all types of athletes train their brains through her business, and she can make even the nerdiest psychology studies understandable and applicable for triathletes.

What we gifted (and why): When we heard about the Muse Athena S Headband, a “brain-sensing headband,” we thought of Daya. The headband claims it can do everything from tracking your brainwave activity for better focus to tracking your blood oxygenation in the prefrontal cortex to help you build mental endurance. If anyone can sort through the science behind the Muse, it’s Daya, so we’re excited to hear how effective it seems to be in her own athletic performance.

Save Big Without Sacrificing Comfort With These Editor-Tested Running Shoes Under $130

💡 Key Takeaways
